via-appia.name: Via Appia
via-appia.t: The Romans called it the queen of roads
via-appia.s: This is the first of Rome's great highways, begun in 312 BC and pushed south until it reached the Adriatic port of Brindisi. Soldiers, traders and travellers all used it to reach the ships for Greece and the East. The paving stones are far too small to see, but south of Rome modern roads still trace its dead-straight line across the flat Pontine plain.
via-appia.w: Look for a ruler-straight road running south-east from Rome across a flat, chequered plain towards the coast at Terracina.
f: It was begun by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus, who gave the road his name.
Near Rome the old road is still lined with tombs and umbrella pines, and parts of the Roman paving survive.
From Brindisi, ships crossed to Dyrrachium, where the Via Egnatia continued east towards Byzantium.

q.q: Which port was the final stop of the Via Appia?

via-egnatia.name: Via Egnatia
via-egnatia.t: Rome's highway across the Balkans to the Bosphorus
via-egnatia.s: Here Rome reached for the East. Built in the 2nd century BC, the Via Egnatia ran from the Adriatic coast of today's Albania over the mountains to Thessaloniki and on to Byzantium. It was the natural sequel to the Via Appia: sail across from Brindisi, then walk. The road itself is invisible from cruise, but you can follow its line past Lake Ohrid and along the Aegean shore.
via-egnatia.w: Find Lake Ohrid among the mountains, then the Gulf of Thessaloniki to the east; the road linked the two and ran on towards Istanbul.
f: It was named after the Roman proconsul Gnaeus Egnatius, who had it built.
From the Adriatic to Byzantium the road covered roughly 1,100 km.
The Apostle Paul travelled along it on his way through Philippi and Thessaloniki.

q.q: Which lake did the Via Egnatia pass on its way east?

via-francigena.name: Via Francigena
via-francigena.t: A medieval pilgrim road from Canterbury to Rome
via-francigena.s: This is the road that medieval pilgrims walked from England to Rome. In 990 Archbishop Sigeric of Canterbury wrote down each overnight stop on his way home from the Pope, and his list still defines the route. It crosses France, climbs the Alps at the Great St Bernard Pass and runs down through Tuscany. From above, trace it by the lakes, passes and river plains it threads between.
via-francigena.w: Look for Lake Geneva, then the high Alpine notch of the Great St Bernard to its south, and the flat Po plain beyond.
f: Sigeric's travel notes list 79 stages between Rome and the English Channel.
The Great St Bernard Pass, at 2,469 m, is the highest point on the route.
Pilgrims still walk it today, collecting stamps in a pilgrim passport.

q.q: Who recorded the stages of the Via Francigena in 990?

camino-frances.name: Camino de Santiago (Camino Francés)
camino-frances.t: A thousand years of footsteps to Santiago
camino-frances.s: This is Europe's best-loved pilgrim road. For more than a thousand years walkers have crossed the Pyrenees here and headed west across northern Spain to the tomb of St James in Santiago de Compostela, about 780 km away. From the air the route is easy to imagine: green mountains at both ends, and between them the Meseta, a high, flat plateau of golden wheat around Burgos and León.
camino-frances.w: Look for the wide tawny plateau between Burgos and León, with the green Galician hills rising to the west.
f: The scallop shell, symbol of St James, marks the way on walls and signposts.
In 1987 it became the first Cultural Route of the Council of Europe.
Hundreds of thousands of people now finish the pilgrimage each year.

q.q: Which symbol marks the Camino de Santiago?

amber-road.name: Amber Road
amber-road.t: Baltic gold carried south to Rome
amber-road.s: Imagine the Baltic shore as a gold mine. Amber washed up on its beaches, and for thousands of years traders carried it south through the Moravian Gate to the Danube and down to Aquileia on the Adriatic, where Roman workshops turned it into jewellery. The route itself left no line you can see, but its two ends are clear: the long sandy spits of the Baltic and the northern Adriatic coast.
amber-road.w: At the northern end, look for the thin sandy spits and lagoons of the Baltic coast near Gdańsk and Kaliningrad.
f: Amber is fossilised tree resin, and Baltic amber is roughly 40 million years old.
Pliny the Elder tells of a Roman knight sent by Nero to the Baltic to buy amber in bulk.
Most of the world's mined amber still comes from the coast near Kaliningrad.

q.q: What is amber?

hadrians-wall.name: Hadrian's Wall
hadrians-wall.t: Rome's northern frontier, coast to coast
hadrians-wall.s: Across the narrow neck of northern England, Emperor Hadrian ordered a stone wall in AD 122. It ran from the Tyne to the Solway Firth, with small forts every Roman mile and garrisons drawn from all over the empire. The wall is only a few metres wide and cannot be seen from cruise, but the gap it guarded, between two estuaries, is plain.
hadrians-wall.w: Trace the land from the Tyne estuary at Newcastle westward to the broad silver Solway Firth beyond Carlisle.
f: The wall was about 117 km long, or 80 Roman miles.
Letters on wooden tablets found at nearby Vindolanda include a birthday party invitation from about AD 100.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1987.

q.q: Roughly how long was Hadrian's Wall?

limes-germanicus.name: Upper Germanic–Raetian Limes
limes-germanicus.t: Rome's frontier line from the Rhine to the Danube
limes-germanicus.s: Here ran the edge of the Roman world. From the Rhine near Koblenz to the Danube near Regensburg, a palisade, ditch and hundreds of watchtowers marked where the empire ended and free Germania began. Much of it lies in forest today, invisible from any height. What you can see are the two great rivers it joined, and the wooded hills of the Taunus and Odenwald between them.
limes-germanicus.w: Find the Rhine and the Danube; the frontier cut across the wooded uplands between them in a long, bent line.
f: The frontier ran about 550 km and had some 900 watchtowers and 60 forts.
One section runs almost perfectly straight for about 80 km, ignoring hills and valleys.
At Saalburg near Frankfurt, a Roman fort was rebuilt around 1900 on its original foundations.

q.q: Which two rivers did this Roman frontier connect?

danube-limes.name: Danube Limes
danube-limes.t: The river that was Rome's frontier
danube-limes.s: For four centuries this river was a border. The Romans lined the Danube with forts and watchtowers, and several of today's capitals grew from their camps: Vienna, Budapest and Belgrade among them. Unlike most Roman frontiers, this one is easy to follow from the air, because the river itself was the line. Watch for the gorge of the Iron Gates, where the Danube squeezes through the Carpathians.
danube-limes.w: Follow the broad Danube; the narrow Iron Gates gorge between Serbia and Romania is the most striking stretch.
f: Vienna grew from the Roman camp of Vindobona, and Budapest from Aquincum.
Trajan's Bridge across the Danube, finished in AD 105, was over a kilometre long.
Its stone piers stood near today's Drobeta-Turnu Severin, and a few stumps still rise on the banks.

q.q: Which capital grew from the Roman camp of Vindobona?

hanseatic-route.name: Hanseatic trade route (London–Novgorod)
hanseatic-route.t: Merchant towns that ruled the northern seas
hanseatic-route.s: This was the old sea road of the Hanseatic League, a merchant alliance that for centuries controlled trade across the North Sea and the Baltic. Its ships carried cloth west to east, and furs, wax, grain and fish the other way, linking offices in London, Bruges, Bergen and Novgorod. Look for the Baltic coast: the red-brick port towns along it were built on this trade.
hanseatic-route.w: Follow the Baltic coast from Lübeck Bay eastward, with the long island of Gotland out to sea.
f: Lübeck was the league's leading city, often called the Queen of the Hanse.
Hamburg's car plates still begin with HH, for Hansestadt Hamburg.
The Hanseatic Diet, the league's assembly, last met in 1669.

q.q: What does HH on Hamburg car plates stand for?

via-domitia.name: Via Domitia
via-domitia.t: The first Roman road in Gaul, Italy to Spain
via-domitia.s: This was the first road Rome built in Gaul, laid out from 118 BC to link Italy with Spain. It climbed over the Alps at Montgenèvre, followed the Durance valley, crossed the Rhône near Beaucaire and ran along the coast plain past Nîmes and Narbonne to the Pyrenees. The road is invisible now, but the valleys, the river and the lagoon-fringed coast still show its path.
via-domitia.w: Look for the Rhône delta and the chain of lagoons along the coast west of it, towards the Pyrenees.
f: It was named after Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus, the Roman general who had it built.
In Narbonne a stretch of the original paving has been uncovered in the town's main square.
The Pont Julien, a Roman bridge near Apt, carried traffic on this route for about 2,000 years.

q.q: Which two lands did the Via Domitia link?

canal-du-midi.name: Canal du Midi
canal-du-midi.t: A 17th-century shortcut from Atlantic to Mediterranean
canal-du-midi.s: Here a 17th-century engineer joined two seas. Pierre-Paul Riquet's canal runs from Toulouse to the Mediterranean, and with the Garonne it links the Atlantic to the Mediterranean without sailing round Spain. Its genius lies in the water supply, collected from the Montagne Noire and fed in at the canal's summit. At about 20 m wide it is too narrow to spot from cruise, but its corridor is clear.
canal-du-midi.w: Look for the lowland corridor between the Pyrenees and the Massif Central, from Toulouse to the Étang de Thau lagoon.
f: The canal is about 240 km long and still in use, now mostly by holiday boats.
At Béziers a staircase of eight locks lifts boats up a single hillside.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1996.

q.q: Who built the Canal du Midi?

kiel-canal.name: Kiel Canal
kiel-canal.t: A shortcut that slices Germany's neck
kiel-canal.s: Look for a straight silver thread crossing the flat farmland of northern Germany. This is the Kiel Canal, opened in 1895 to link the North Sea with the Baltic so that ships no longer had to sail round Denmark. It runs 98 km from the Elbe estuary to Kiel. At about 100 m wide, it can be picked out from cruise height on a clear day.
kiel-canal.w: A thin straight waterline running north-east from the Elbe mouth at Brunsbüttel to the fjord at Kiel.
f: By the number of ships, it is one of the busiest artificial waterways in the world.
The shortcut saves ships about 460 km compared with the voyage round Denmark.
At Rendsburg a transporter bridge from 1913 carries a gondola hanging beneath the railway.

q.q: Which peninsula does the Kiel Canal let ships avoid?

orient-express.name: Orient Express route
orient-express.t: The legendary sleeper train from Paris to Constantinople
orient-express.s: Along this line ran the most famous train in Europe. From 1883 the Orient Express carried passengers in sleeping cars from Paris towards Constantinople, and from 1889 all the way there by rail, through Munich, Vienna, Budapest and Belgrade. It made crossing half a continent feel like a stay in a grand hotel. From above, follow the Danube, then the Balkan valleys down to the Bosphorus.
orient-express.w: Follow the Danube past Vienna and Budapest, then valleys through Serbia and Bulgaria towards the Bosphorus.
f: The train was created by the Belgian entrepreneur Georges Nagelmackers.
Istanbul's Sirkeci station, opened in 1890, was built as its terminus.
The through service from Paris to Istanbul ended in 1977.

q.q: Who founded the company that ran the Orient Express?

bleriot-channel-1909.name: Blériot's Channel flight (1909)
bleriot-channel-1909.t: The flight that shrank the English Channel
bleriot-channel-1909.s: On 25 July 1909 Louis Blériot took off from a field near Calais in a small monoplane and landed below Dover Castle about 37 minutes later. It was the first aeroplane flight across the English Channel, just six years after the Wright brothers first flew. He had no compass. The strait, with its white cliffs and busy shipping lanes, suddenly looked much narrower.
bleriot-channel-1909.w: Look for the white chalk cliffs at Dover facing the flat French coast near Calais, about 35 km apart.
f: The flight won Blériot a £1,000 prize from London's Daily Mail.
A granite outline of his aeroplane marks the landing spot near Dover Castle.
His aircraft, the Blériot XI, is now in the Musée des Arts et Métiers in Paris.

q.q: How long did Blériot's Channel flight take?

paris-meridian-arc.name: Paris meridian arc (the metre survey)
paris-meridian-arc.t: Where the metre was measured on the ground
paris-meridian-arc.s: This line gave the world the metre. In the 1790s two astronomers, Delambre and Méchain, measured the distance from Dunkirk to Barcelona by chains of triangles between church towers and hilltops. From it they fixed the metre as one ten-millionth of the distance from pole to equator. The line runs almost due north–south through Paris, invisible but exact.
paris-meridian-arc.w: The arc runs nearly due north–south through Paris, from the Channel coast at Dunkirk to Barcelona.
f: Delambre measured the northern half and Méchain the southern half, meeting at Rodez.
The result was cast as a platinum bar, the Metre of the Archives, in 1799.
They slightly misjudged the Earth's flattening, so their metre came out about 0.2 mm short.

q.q: Which unit was this survey meant to define?

ancient-rome.name: Ancient Rome
ancient-rome.t: The city whose roads led everywhere
ancient-rome.s: This was the heart of an empire that stretched from Scotland to Syria. At its peak ancient Rome was home to perhaps a million people, and its Forum, Colosseum and Pantheon still stand in the middle of the modern city. From cruise height the monuments merge into the sprawl, but the Tiber's lazy S-bends through the centre are the same river the city was founded on.
ancient-rome.w: Find the Tiber winding through the city in tight bends, about 25 km inland from the coast at Ostia.
f: The Colosseum, opened in AD 80, could hold around 50,000 spectators.
The Pantheon's concrete dome, nearly 2,000 years old, is still the largest unreinforced one in the world.
By tradition, Rome was founded on 21 April 753 BC, and the city still celebrates that date.

q.q: In which year, by tradition, was Rome founded?

pompeii.name: Pompeii and Herculaneum
pompeii.t: Roman towns kept under ash for 1,700 years
pompeii.s: Look for the cone of Vesuvius above the Bay of Naples. In AD 79 it buried two Roman towns under ash and mud, and in doing so kept them almost intact: painted walls, bakeries, shop signs, even scribbled graffiti. Today they are the fullest picture we have of everyday Roman life. The streets are too small to see from here, but the volcano that made them famous is unmistakable.
pompeii.w: A broad volcanic cone with a dark crater, rising just east of the Bay of Naples; the ruins lie at its foot.
f: Excavations at Pompeii began in 1748, and about a third of the town is still unexcavated.
Its walls are covered in ancient graffiti, from election slogans to jokes.
Charred papyrus scrolls from Herculaneum are now being read with X-ray scans and AI.

q.q: Which volcano buried Pompeii?

acropolis-athens.name: Acropolis of Athens
acropolis-athens.t: The rock where Western architecture found its form
acropolis-athens.s: In the middle of the Athens basin rises a flat-topped rock crowned with marble temples. The Parthenon was built on it in the 5th century BC, when Athens was experimenting with democracy, and its proportions have been copied on banks, museums and parliaments ever since. The temple itself is too small to pick out from cruise, but the city's bowl between the mountains and the sea is easy to see.
acropolis-athens.w: Look for a sprawling pale city in a bowl of mountains, opening south-west onto the Saronic Gulf and Piraeus.
f: The Parthenon was built between 447 and 432 BC and dedicated to Athena.
Its columns bulge slightly and its floor curves upward, so it looks perfectly straight to the eye.
The marble came from Mount Pentelicus, about 16 km away.

q.q: To which goddess was the Parthenon dedicated?

delphi.name: Delphi
delphi.t: The ancient Greeks' centre of the world
delphi.s: Look for the massif of Mount Parnassus, often white on top, above the Gulf of Corinth. On its southern slope sat Delphi, where for a thousand years Greeks came to ask Apollo's oracle about wars, colonies and marriages. They believed it marked the centre of the world. The temple terraces are invisible from here, but the mountain and the silvery olive plain running down to the sea are clear.
delphi.w: A high, often snowy mountain block north of the Gulf of Corinth, with a wide olive plain below its south side.
f: A carved stone called the omphalos, or navel, marked Delphi as the centre of the world.
The Pythian Games held here included music and poetry contests as well as athletics.
Winners of the Pythian Games were crowned with laurel, the plant sacred to Apollo.

q.q: Which god's oracle spoke at Delphi?

olympia.name: Olympia
olympia.s: In a green valley in the western Peloponnese, the ancient Greeks held the Olympic Games for more than a thousand years. Wars were paused so athletes could travel safely, and victors went home with an olive wreath and lasting fame. Every modern Olympic flame is still lit here from the sun's rays. From cruise, look for the wide Alfeios river valley winding to the Ionian Sea.
olympia.w: Find the broad valley of the Alfeios river running west to the Ionian coast in the western Peloponnese.
f: By tradition the first Games were held in 776 BC.
The stadium track is about 192 m long, the length of an ancient stade.
Its gold-and-ivory statue of Zeus was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

q.q: What did ancient Olympic victors receive?

knossos.name: Knossos
knossos.t: The palace behind the legend of the labyrinth
knossos.s: Just inland from Heraklion on Crete's north coast stood the greatest palace of Europe's first advanced civilisation, the Minoans. Its maze of rooms, light wells and painted walls may lie behind the Greek myth of King Minos, the labyrinth and the Minotaur. From above you won't see the ruins, but you can see Crete's long mountainous spine and the busy coast where the Minoans built their sea-trading world.
knossos.w: On Crete's north coast, look for the city of Heraklion; the palace lies a few kilometres inland to its south.
f: The British archaeologist Arthur Evans excavated Knossos from 1900.
Evans rebuilt parts of the palace in concrete, which is still debated today.
Clay tablets from Knossos written in Linear B turned out to be an early form of Greek.

q.q: Who excavated Knossos from 1900?

mycenae.name: Mycenae
mycenae.t: The citadel of Homer's King Agamemnon
mycenae.s: On a hill above the Argolid plain stood Mycenae, the fortress that gave its name to Greece's Late Bronze Age. Homer made it the home of King Agamemnon, leader of the Greeks at Troy. Its walls are built of boulders so huge that later Greeks thought giants had laid them. From cruise, look for the flat green plain of Argos opening onto its gulf.
mycenae.w: Find the Gulf of Argolis in the north-east Peloponnese; the citadel stands on the plain's northern edge.
f: The walls are called Cyclopean, after the one-eyed giants said to have built them.
Its famous Lion Gate, carved around 1250 BC, is one of the oldest monumental sculptures in Europe.
The gold 'Mask of Agamemnon' found here in 1876 is about 300 years older than the Trojan War of legend.

q.q: What guards the main entrance to Mycenae?

stonehenge.name: Stonehenge and Avebury
stonehenge.t: Stone circles aligned with the midsummer sun
stonehenge.s: On the rolling chalk of Salisbury Plain stands the world's most famous prehistoric monument. Stonehenge was built in stages over some 1,500 years; its axis points to sunrise at midsummer and sunset at midwinter. Nearby Avebury has an even larger stone circle, with a village built inside it. The stones are far too small to see from here, but the pale downland is easy to spot.
stonehenge.w: Look for open, pale-green chalk downland north of Salisbury, with few trees and scattered military ranges.
f: Its smaller bluestones were brought about 240 km from the Preseli Hills in Wales.
The biggest sarsen stones weigh around 25–30 tonnes each.
Avebury's outer circle is so big that part of the village sits inside it.

q.q: Where did Stonehenge's bluestones come from?

carnac.name: Carnac stones
carnac.t: Rows of standing stones marching across Brittany
carnac.s: On the south coast of Brittany, thousands of standing stones stand in long parallel rows, some stretching more than a kilometre. They were raised in the Neolithic, long before Stonehenge's great sarsens, and nobody knows exactly why. Local legend says they are Roman soldiers turned to stone. The rows are too small to see, but the Quiberon peninsula and the island-studded Gulf of Morbihan are plain.
carnac.w: Look for the thin Quiberon peninsula pointing south, with the island-filled Gulf of Morbihan just east of it.
f: More than 3,000 standing stones survive around Carnac.
The Ménec alignment alone has over 1,000 stones in 11 rows.
The word 'menhir', for a standing stone, comes from Breton: 'long stone'.

q.q: Roughly how many standing stones survive at Carnac?

lascaux.name: Lascaux and the Vézère valley
lascaux.t: Ice Age horses and bulls painted in the dark
lascaux.s: Somewhere in these wooded valleys, a cave holds some of the finest art of the Ice Age: horses, deer and huge black bulls painted about 17,000 years ago. It was found in 1940 by four local teenagers. The Vézère valley around it is packed with prehistoric sites. From the air you see only green limestone hills and a winding river, just as the painters did.
lascaux.w: Look for the meandering Vézère river among wooded limestone hills, north-east of the wider Dordogne valley.
f: The cave holds about 600 paintings and around 1,500 engravings.
It closed to visitors in 1963 to protect the art; people now visit exact replicas nearby.
The Vézère valley has 147 prehistoric sites and 25 decorated caves on UNESCO's list.

q.q: Who found the Lascaux cave in 1940?

newgrange.name: Newgrange (Brú na Bóinne)
newgrange.t: A tomb older than the pyramids, lit by midwinter sun
newgrange.s: In a great bend of the River Boyne, north of Dublin, stands a huge round mound faced with white quartz. Newgrange was built around 3200 BC, before Stonehenge's stone circle and the pyramids of Giza. Once a year, at the midwinter sunrise, a beam of light travels down its passage and lights the inner chamber. The mound is small from here, but the loop of the Boyne is visible.
newgrange.w: Find the River Boyne west of Drogheda; the monuments sit inside a tight southern loop of the river.
f: The sunbeam enters through a 'roof-box' above the doorway and lasts about 17 minutes.
Its passage is about 19 m long and ends in a chamber with a stone corbelled roof.
Neighbouring Knowth has more megalithic art than any other site in western Europe.

q.q: What lights up Newgrange's chamber each year?

skara-brae.name: Neolithic Orkney (Skara Brae)
skara-brae.t: A stone-age village with its furniture still in place
skara-brae.s: On Orkney's main island, a Stone Age village lay hidden under sand until a storm uncovered it in 1850. Skara Brae's houses still have their stone beds, hearths and dressers, left as if their owners had just stepped out. Nearby stand the Ring of Brodgar and the great tomb of Maeshowe. From above, look for Orkney's green, treeless islands and the two lochs at their heart.
skara-brae.w: Look for low green islands north of Scotland's tip; the monuments lie around two joined lochs on the largest one.
f: Skara Brae was lived in for about 600 years.
At midwinter the setting sun shines down the entrance passage of Maeshowe.
The Ring of Brodgar originally had about 60 stones; around 27 still stand.

q.q: What uncovered Skara Brae in 1850?

pont-du-gard.name: Pont du Gard
pont-du-gard.t: Rome's aqueduct bridge, three tiers high
pont-du-gard.s: In the gorge of the Gardon river, a Roman bridge of three stacked arcades carried water to the city of Nîmes. It was one part of an aqueduct about 50 km long that fell only a few metres over its whole length, a feat of surveying. The bridge is too small to see from cruise, but the green Gardon gorge between Nîmes and Avignon is where to look.
pont-du-gard.w: Look between Nîmes and Avignon, where the Gardon river cuts a green gorge before reaching the Rhône.
f: At about 49 m, it is the tallest aqueduct bridge the Romans built.
The aqueduct drops only about 12 m over its 50 km, around 25 cm per kilometre.
The stones were laid without mortar in the main arches.

q.q: Which Roman city did the Pont du Gard supply?

mont-saint-michel.name: Mont-Saint-Michel
mont-saint-michel.t: An abbey on a rock, cut off by the tide
mont-saint-michel.s: Look for a vast grey-and-silver bay on the Normandy–Brittany border. In its middle sits a tiny rocky island topped by a Gothic abbey, founded as a Benedictine monastery in 966. The bay has some of the biggest tides in Europe, and at high water the sea surrounds the rock. From cruise the abbey is a dot, but the patterned sandflats and river channels are striking.
mont-saint-michel.w: A broad bay of sandflats and winding channels where Normandy meets Brittany, with a small island near its southern shore.
f: The tidal range in the bay can reach about 14 m.
In 2014 a light bridge replaced the old causeway so the sea can flow around the rock again.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1979, with its bay.

q.q: How high can the tide rise in Mont-Saint-Michel Bay?

aachen.name: Aachen, Charlemagne's capital
aachen.t: The spa town where Charlemagne ruled Europe
aachen.s: Near the corner where Germany, Belgium and the Netherlands meet lies Aachen, Charlemagne's favourite residence. Around 800 he built a domed chapel here that became the heart of his empire, and for six centuries German kings were crowned in it. The Romans had come for the hot springs, which still flow. From above, look for the city on the edge of the green Eifel uplands.
aachen.w: Look for the city just east of where Germany, Belgium and the Netherlands meet, at the edge of wooded uplands.
f: About 30 German kings were crowned in Aachen between 936 and 1531.
In 1978 its cathedral was among the first 12 sites on UNESCO's World Heritage list.
The Roman name Aquae Granni referred to the town's hot springs.

q.q: Whose chapel became Aachen Cathedral?

ravenna.name: Ravenna
ravenna.t: The last capital of the Western Roman Empire
ravenna.s: On the flat Adriatic coast of Italy, Ravenna was for a time the capital of the Western Roman Empire, then of Ostrogothic kings and Byzantine governors. They filled its churches with glittering mosaics that still look fresh after 1,500 years, among the finest anywhere. The city was once a harbour; the sea has since retreated. From above, look for the flat coast, pine woods and lagoons.
ravenna.w: Look for a low, straight coastline with dark pine forests and, to the north, the wide lagoons of Comacchio.
f: The Western Roman emperors moved their court to Ravenna in 402.
The mosaics of San Vitale show Emperor Justinian and Empress Theodora with their courts.
The poet Dante died in Ravenna in 1321 and is buried there.

q.q: Which poet is buried in Ravenna?

venice-republic.name: Republic of Venice
venice-republic.t: A merchant republic built on a lagoon
venice-republic.s: Look for a fish-shaped city floating in a lagoon, joined to the mainland by a long bridge. For about a thousand years Venice was an independent republic ruled by elected doges, and its galleys carried spices, silk and glass between Europe and the East. Few places are as easy to recognise from the air: the lagoon, the barrier islands and the city's dense tangle of canals.
venice-republic.w: A compact fish-shaped city in a shallow lagoon, linked to the mainland by a long straight causeway.
f: The city stands on more than 100 small islands linked by around 400 bridges.
Its Arsenal was one of the largest shipyards of the pre-industrial world.
Marco Polo, whose travels made China famous in Europe, was a Venetian merchant.

q.q: Who ended the Venetian Republic in 1797?

split-diocletian.name: Diocletian's Palace, Split
split-diocletian.t: An emperor's retirement home that became a city
split-diocletian.s: When Emperor Diocletian gave up the throne around AD 305, he retired to a fortress-palace he had built on the Dalmatian coast. After Rome fell, local people moved inside its walls, and a whole town grew within them. Today shops, homes and a cathedral fill the Roman palace. From above, look for Split on its peninsula, facing the long islands of Brač and Hvar.
split-diocletian.w: A city on a peninsula of the Croatian coast, with the long islands of Brač and Hvar lying offshore.
f: Diocletian was the first Roman emperor to step down of his own accord.
Split's cathedral was built in the emperor's own mausoleum.
Around 3,000 people still live inside the old palace walls.

q.q: Which emperor retired to a palace at Split?

constantinople.name: Constantinople
constantinople.s: This is the city Constantine made the new Rome in 330. As Constantinople it was the capital of the Byzantine Empire for over a thousand years, and then of the Ottoman sultans, guarding the only sea route between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean. Its dome of Hagia Sophia amazed visitors for centuries. From the air, look for the Bosphorus and the curved Golden Horn.
constantinople.w: Look for the narrow Bosphorus strait and the curved inlet of the Golden Horn cutting into the old city.
f: Hagia Sophia, finished in 537, was the world's largest cathedral for nearly a thousand years.
The city's land walls, built in the 5th century, ran about 6 km from sea to sea.
Before Constantine, the city was the Greek colony of Byzantium, founded around 660 BC.

q.q: Which emperor refounded Byzantium as his capital in 330?

alhambra-granada.name: Nasrid Granada and the Alhambra
alhambra-granada.t: A red palace-city under the snowy Sierra Nevada
alhambra-granada.s: Look for the Sierra Nevada, often snow-capped, rising behind the city of Granada. Here the Nasrid dynasty ruled the last Muslim kingdom of the Iberian Peninsula until 1492, and built the Alhambra, a hilltop palace of carved stucco, tiles and courtyard fountains. The palace cannot be seen from cruise, but the mountain wall behind it, higher than any other in mainland Spain, is hard to miss.
alhambra-granada.w: A long mountain range, white-topped in winter and spring, with Granada spread on the plain at its north-western foot.
f: The name Alhambra comes from the Arabic for 'the red one', after the colour of its walls.
The fountain in the Court of the Lions rests on the backs of 12 marble lions.
Mulhacén in the Sierra Nevada, at 3,479 m, is the highest peak in mainland Spain.

q.q: What does the name 'Alhambra' mean?

cordoba-umayyad.name: Umayyad Córdoba
cordoba-umayyad.t: Once one of Europe's greatest cities
cordoba-umayyad.s: In the 10th century Córdoba, on the Guadalquivir, was the capital of an Umayyad caliphate and one of the largest and most learned cities in Europe. Its Great Mosque, with a forest of columns and red-and-white striped arches, still stands, with a cathedral built right in the middle of it. From the air, look for the city on the river, with the dark Sierra Morena rising to the north.
cordoba-umayyad.w: Find the Guadalquivir valley; the city lies on the river at the foot of the wooded Sierra Morena hills.
f: The mosque's prayer hall has over 800 columns of marble, jasper and granite.
A Renaissance cathedral was built inside the mosque in the 16th century.
The ruined palace-city of Medina Azahara lies just west of Córdoba.

q.q: What was built inside Córdoba's Great Mosque?

belem-lisbon.name: Belém, Lisbon: the Age of Discovery
belem-lisbon.t: The riverbank where the sea route to India began
belem-lisbon.s: From this riverbank at the mouth of the Tagus, Portuguese ships set out in the 15th and 16th centuries to map Africa's coast and reach India by sea. Vasco da Gama sailed from here in 1497. Spice money paid for the ornate Jerónimos Monastery and the Belém Tower that guarded the harbour. From above, look for the broad Tagus estuary and the long red suspension bridge across it.
belem-lisbon.w: Look for the wide Tagus estuary opening to the Atlantic, crossed by a long suspension bridge west of Lisbon's centre.
f: Vasco da Gama is buried in the Jerónimos Monastery.
The Belém Tower was completed around 1519 to guard the harbour entrance.
The monastery's intricate style, called Manueline, uses carved ropes, shells and sea creatures.

q.q: Who sailed from Belém in 1497 to find a sea route to India?

bergen-bryggen.name: Bryggen, Bergen
bergen-bryggen.t: The Hanseatic wharf of wooden gables
bergen-bryggen.s: In the city of Bergen, surrounded by fjords and mountains, German merchants of the Hanseatic League ran one of their four great foreign offices for almost 400 years. They traded grain for stockfish, cod dried on racks in the Arctic wind. Their row of tall wooden gabled houses, Bryggen, still lines the harbour. From above, look for the city on its inlet, ringed by steep hills.
bergen-bryggen.w: A city on a sheltered inlet of Norway's west coast, ringed by steep hills and fjords, often under cloud.
f: The stockfish came from the Lofoten Islands, hundreds of kilometres to the north.
Bryggen has burned several times and was rebuilt after a fire in 1702 in the old style.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1979.

q.q: What did Bergen's Hanseatic merchants mainly export?

visby.name: Visby
visby.t: A walled Hanseatic town in the middle of the Baltic
visby.s: On the west coast of Gotland, in the middle of the Baltic, stands Visby, a Hanseatic trading town still enclosed by its medieval wall. Its merchants grew rich on trade between Russia and western Europe, and filled the town with stone churches, many now roofless ruins. From the air, look for the long, low island of Gotland, the largest in Sweden.
visby.w: A long, low limestone island in the open Baltic; Visby lies on its western shore, facing Sweden.
f: Visby's ring wall is about 3.4 km long and still has 27 of its towers.
Gotland has yielded more Viking-age silver hoards than anywhere else in Scandinavia.
The town became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1995.

q.q: On which island does Visby stand?

thingvellir.name: Þingvellir
thingvellir.t: An open-air parliament in a crack between continents
thingvellir.s: North-east of Reykjavík lies a lake in a rift valley where two tectonic plates pull apart. In 930 Iceland's settlers began meeting here each summer for the Althing, an open-air assembly that made laws and settled disputes. It gathered here until 1798. From above you can see what they could not: the lake and the long fissures running through the lava, where North America and Eurasia drift apart.
thingvellir.w: Look for Iceland's largest natural lake, north-east of Reykjavík, with dark lava fissures running along its north shore.
f: The Althing is often called one of the oldest parliaments in the world.
In the year 1000 the assembly here decided that Iceland would adopt Christianity.
Across Iceland, the two plates drift apart by about 2 cm a year.

q.q: In which year was the Althing founded?

gutenberg-mainz.name: Mainz, Gutenberg's press
gutenberg-mainz.t: Where movable type began Europe's print revolution
gutenberg-mainz.s: Look for the point where the Main flows into the Rhine. On its west bank lies Mainz, where around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg began printing with movable metal type. His Bible, finished around 1455, showed books could be made in hundreds of copies instead of one at a time. Within 50 years printing presses were running in hundreds of European towns. The confluence is easy to spot.
gutenberg-mainz.w: Find the confluence of the Main and the Rhine, with Mainz on the west bank and Wiesbaden opposite.
f: About 180 copies of the Gutenberg Bible were printed; 49 are known to survive.
Gutenberg's system combined metal type, oil-based ink and a press adapted from wine presses.
Mainz began as the Roman fortress of Mogontiacum.

q.q: Which book did Gutenberg print around 1455?

greenwich-meridian.name: Greenwich prime meridian
greenwich-meridian.t: Longitude zero, the line every map counts from
greenwich-meridian.s: On a hill above the Thames stands the Royal Observatory, founded in 1675. In 1884 delegates from 25 nations agreed that its meridian would be longitude zero for the world. Every position on your flight map is measured east or west of it, and world time was once counted from it. From above, look for the Thames looping round the Isle of Dogs; Greenwich lies on the south bank.
greenwich-meridian.w: Look for the Thames's tight loop around the Isle of Dogs in east London; Greenwich Park lies just south of it.
f: The Royal Observatory was founded by King Charles II in 1675.
The zero line used by GPS lies about 100 m east of the brass line at the observatory.
The 1884 decision was made at a conference in Washington, D.C.

q.q: When was Greenwich chosen as the prime meridian?

montgolfier-annonay.name: Annonay, the first hot-air balloon
montgolfier-annonay.t: Where two paper-makers launched the age of flight
montgolfier-annonay.s: In the hills west of the Rhône lies Annonay, home of the Montgolfier brothers, paper-makers. On 4 June 1783 they filled a large cloth-and-paper envelope with hot air in the town square and watched it rise more than a kilometre. Within months their balloons carried a sheep, a duck and a rooster, and then the first human passengers. Every flight since traces back here.
montgolfier-annonay.w: Look for the Rhône valley running south from Lyon; Annonay lies in the wooded hills a little to its west.
f: The first human flight in a Montgolfier balloon took place over Paris on 21 November 1783.
At Versailles in September 1783, a sheep, a duck and a rooster flew and landed safely.
In French, a hot-air balloon is still called a 'montgolfière'.

q.q: What was the Montgolfier family's trade?

ironbridge.name: Ironbridge Gorge
ironbridge.t: A valley that helped start the Industrial Revolution
ironbridge.s: In this wooded gorge of the River Severn, the Industrial Revolution found its fuel and its symbol. In 1709 Abraham Darby first smelted iron with coke instead of charcoal, making iron cheap. In 1779 his grandson raised the world's first major cast-iron bridge across the river. The bridge is too small to see from cruise, but the Severn's deep valley west of Telford is visible.
ironbridge.w: Find the River Severn winding south-east from Shrewsbury; the gorge lies just south of the new town of Telford.
f: The Iron Bridge has a span of about 30 m and is still standing.
Its parts were joined with carpentry techniques, such as dovetails, because iron building was so new.
The gorge became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1986.

q.q: What is the Iron Bridge made of?

malta-temples.name: Megalithic temples of Malta
malta-temples.t: Stone temples older than the pyramids
malta-temples.s: On the small islands of Malta and Gozo, farmers of the Stone Age built great stone temples more than 5,000 years ago, earlier than Stonehenge's circle or the pyramids of Giza. They are among the oldest free-standing buildings on Earth. The temples are too small to see, but the islands themselves, golden-brown in the blue Mediterranean south of Sicily, are easy to find.
malta-temples.w: Look for two small golden-brown islands, Malta and Gozo, about 90 km south of Sicily.
f: Local legend says the Ġgantija temples on Gozo were built by a giantess.
The Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum is an underground temple and burial site cut into solid rock.
Seven of the temples are on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

q.q: Who, in local legend, built the Ġgantija temples?

etruria.name: Etruria
etruria.t: Land of the Etruscans, Rome's mysterious teachers
etruria.s: This is the land of the Etruscans, who ruled central Italy before Rome and taught the young city much of its religion, engineering and style. They built hill towns, drained marshes and painted their tombs with banquets, dancers and musicians. Their language is still only partly understood. From above, look for the green Tuscan hills and the round volcanic lakes that dot the land north of Rome.
etruria.w: Look for round crater lakes such as Bolsena and Bracciano among green hills between Rome and Florence.
f: Tuscany takes its name from the Etruscans, whom the Romans called Tusci.
The painted tombs of Tarquinia and Cerveteri are on the UNESCO World Heritage list.
Lake Bolsena fills an old volcanic caldera and is the largest volcanic lake in Europe.

q.q: Which Italian region is named after the Etruscans?

magna-graecia.name: Magna Graecia
magna-graecia.t: When southern Italy was part of the Greek world
magna-graecia.s: From the 8th century BC, Greek settlers sailed west and founded cities along the coasts of southern Italy and Sicily, so many that the Romans called the region Greater Greece. Pythagoras taught here, and cities like Syracuse and Taranto rivalled Athens. From above, look for the boot's toe and heel and the deep Gulf of Taranto between them, the sea the colonists crossed.
magna-graecia.w: Look for the toe and heel of Italy's boot, with the wide Gulf of Taranto curving between them.
f: Naples began as the Greek colony of Neapolis, 'the new city'.
The word 'sybarite', for a lover of luxury, comes from the rich colony of Sybaris.
The Doric temples at Paestum are among the best-preserved Greek temples anywhere.

q.q: What does Naples' Greek name, Neapolis, mean?

nuragic-sardinia.name: Nuragic Sardinia
nuragic-sardinia.t: An island of thousands of Bronze Age stone towers
nuragic-sardinia.s: Sardinia is dotted with stone towers called nuraghi, built by a Bronze Age people who left no writing. Thousands survive, from single cones to fortress-villages with walls and courtyards, and archaeologists still debate what they were for. The towers are too small to see from cruise, but the island's rugged granite mountains and empty uplands, where many of them stand, are easy to see.
nuragic-sardinia.w: A large, rugged, lightly populated island south of Corsica, with granite mountains in the east.
f: More than 7,000 nuraghi are known across the island.
Su Nuraxi at Barumini, a nuraghe village, became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1997.
Nuragic smiths made small bronze figures of warriors, priests and animals.

q.q: What is a nuraghe?

al-andalus.name: Al-Andalus
al-andalus.s: For almost eight centuries much of the Iberian Peninsula was al-Andalus, ruled by Muslim dynasties from Córdoba, Seville and Granada. Its scholars preserved and extended Greek learning, and its farmers brought rice, oranges and sugar cane to Europe. Christians, Muslims and Jews lived side by side, not always peacefully. From above, look for the Guadalquivir valley and the endless dotted rows of olive trees around it.
al-andalus.w: Look for the broad Guadalquivir valley and hillsides covered in regular dotted rows of olive groves.
f: The philosophers Averroes and Maimonides were both born in Córdoba in the 12th century.
The name of the region of Andalusia comes from al-Andalus.
Many Spanish words, such as 'aceite' (oil) and 'azúcar' (sugar), come from Arabic.

q.q: Which Spanish region takes its name from al-Andalus?

dacia.name: Dacia
dacia.t: The gold-rich mountain kingdom inside the Carpathians
dacia.s: Inside the great curve of the Carpathians lay Dacia, a kingdom of mountain fortresses and gold mines. In AD 106 it became a Roman province under Trajan, and for the next 165 years Roman settlers mixed with the Dacians. Their Latin grew into Romanian. From above, look for the arc of the Carpathians, often snow-streaked, wrapped around the green Transylvanian plateau.
dacia.w: Look for the curved chain of the Carpathians enclosing a broad, rolling plateau of farms and forest.
f: The Dacian capital, Sarmizegetusa Regia, stood at about 1,200 m in the Orăștie Mountains.
Trajan's Column in Rome tells the story of the Roman campaigns in Dacia in a spiral of carved scenes.
The Romans withdrew from Dacia around AD 271.

q.q: Which language grew from the Latin spoken in Dacia?

sapmi.name: Sápmi, land of the Sámi
sapmi.t: Homeland of the Sámi, across four countries
sapmi.s: This is Sápmi, the homeland of the Sámi, the Indigenous people of the far north of Europe. It spans Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia's Kola Peninsula. For centuries many Sámi followed reindeer between winter forests and summer pastures by the coast and in the fells, and some still do. From above you see their landscape: lakes, bogs, birch and pine, and long winter snow.
sapmi.w: Look for a vast land of lakes, low fells and forest, white for much of the year, north of the Gulf of Bothnia.
f: Sámi National Day, 6 February, marks the first Sámi assembly held in Trondheim in 1917.
Norway, Sweden and Finland each have an elected Sámi Parliament.
The joik is a traditional Sámi song, often sung to evoke a person or a place.

q.q: What is a joik?

incense-route.name: Incense Route
incense-route.t: Camel caravans carrying frankincense to Rome
incense-route.s: This was the road of frankincense and myrrh. Camel caravans carried these precious resins from the south of Arabia north along the Red Sea hills, oasis to oasis, to Petra and the Mediterranean port of Gaza. Temples across the ancient world burned incense, so the trade made the desert kingdoms rich. From above you see what the caravans crossed: bare mountains, lava fields and sand.
incense-route.w: Look for dark volcanic hills and sandy valleys running north–south inland from the Red Sea coast.
f: Frankincense is the dried resin of a small desert tree, Boswellia.
The Nabataeans of Petra grew rich by taxing and guiding the caravans.
The caravan journey from southern Arabia to Gaza took around two months.

q.q: What is frankincense?

royal-road.name: Persian Royal Road
royal-road.t: The highway of the Persian kings, Sardis to Susa
royal-road.s: In the 5th century BC the Persian king Darius the Great linked the edges of his empire with a road about 2,700 km long, from Sardis near the Aegean to his capital at Susa. Relay stations with fresh horses lined the way, so royal messengers could cross it in about a week. From above, trace it across the Anatolian plateau, over the Euphrates and Tigris and down to the plains of Iran.
royal-road.w: Across eastern Turkey, look for the upper Euphrates and Tigris valleys the road crossed on its way to Mesopotamia.
f: Herodotus wrote that travellers on foot needed about 90 days for the full journey.
He counted 111 relay stations along the road.
His praise of the couriers, that neither snow nor rain stayed them, is carved on a New York post office.

q.q: Which Persian king built the Royal Road?

suez-canal.name: Suez Canal
suez-canal.t: A ruler-straight line joining two seas
suez-canal.s: Look for a thin straight line cutting through the desert between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. Opened in 1869, the Suez Canal spared ships the long voyage round Africa. It has no locks: the sea simply flows through, pausing in the Bitter Lakes halfway. From cruise height it is one of the clearest human-made lines on Earth, often with a convoy of ships strung along it.
suez-canal.w: A straight blue line from Port Said south to Suez, widening into the Great Bitter Lake halfway along.
f: The canal was built under the French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps.
It is about 193 km long and was later widened, with a parallel channel added along part of it in 2015.
It cut the sea route between Britain and India by about 40 percent.

q.q: Who led the building of the Suez Canal?

troy.name: Troy
troy.s: At the mouth of the Dardanelles lies the mound of Troy. For thousands of years people rebuilt a city here, layer on layer, and one of those cities may be the Troy of Homer's Iliad. It guarded the sea route between the Aegean and the Black Sea. The mound is too small to see, but the narrow strait and the river plain beside it are clear.
troy.w: Look for the entrance of the Dardanelles strait; the site lies just inland on its Asian side, above a flat river plain.
f: Archaeologists have found at least nine cities built on top of one another.
Heinrich Schliemann's 'Priam's Treasure' turned out to be about a thousand years older than Homer's Troy.
Troy became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1998.

q.q: Who began excavating Troy in the 1870s?

ephesus.name: Ephesus
ephesus.t: A great Roman port now stranded far inland
ephesus.s: Ephesus was one of the largest cities of the Roman East, with a marble main street, a theatre for about 25,000 people and the grand Library of Celsus. It was a port, but the river silted up its harbour, and the coast now lies kilometres away. From above you can read that story: a flat green plain of river silt where the sea once came in, west of the town of Selçuk.
ephesus.w: Look for a flat green river plain west of Selçuk that runs out to the sea near Kuşadası.
f: Its Temple of Artemis was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
The front of the Library of Celsus, built in the 2nd century AD, has been rebuilt from its original stones.
Ephesus became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2015.

q.q: Which Wonder of the Ancient World stood at Ephesus?

pergamon.name: Pergamon
pergamon.t: A hilltop capital that gave its name to parchment
pergamon.s: On a steep hill above the town of Bergama stood Pergamon, capital of a rich Hellenistic kingdom. Its kings built a great library, a famous altar and one of the steepest theatres of the ancient world, cut into the slope. The library needed so much writing material that Pergamon became known for parchment. From above, look for the green plain of the Bakırçay river, inland from the Aegean.
pergamon.w: Look for the Bakırçay river plain about 25 km inland from the Aegean coast, north of İzmir.
f: The word 'parchment' comes from the name of Pergamon.
The Pergamon Altar was taken to Berlin in the 19th century and gave its name to a museum there.
The theatre's seating drops down the hillside in about 80 rows.

q.q: Which writing material is named after Pergamon?

sardis.name: Sardis, city of the first coins
sardis.s: In this fertile valley stood Sardis, capital of the Lydian kingdom. Around the 7th century BC the Lydians began stamping lumps of electrum, a natural gold–silver alloy, into coins, one of the first uses of coinage anywhere. Their last king, Croesus, became a byword for wealth. The city later marked the start of the Persian Royal Road. From above, look for the broad green Gediz valley east of İzmir.
sardis.w: Look for the broad green Gediz valley east of İzmir, with a mountain ridge rising along its southern side.
f: The river Pactolus, which ran through Sardis, was said to carry gold dust.
The phrase 'as rich as Croesus' comes from the last king of Lydia.
The ruins include one of the largest ancient synagogues ever found.

q.q: Which king of Sardis became a byword for wealth?

gobekli-tepe.name: Göbekli Tepe
gobekli-tepe.s: On a hill above the Harran plain, hunter-gatherers raised great stone pillars carved with foxes, snakes and vultures about 11,500 years ago. That is before pottery, before writing, and before farming had taken hold. Göbekli Tepe turned the old idea that villages came first and monuments later upside down. The pillars are invisible from cruise, but the wide, now irrigated plain around Şanlıurfa is easy to see.
gobekli-tepe.w: Look for the wide plain north of the Syrian border near Şanlıurfa, green in patches with irrigated fields.
f: Its T-shaped pillars stand up to about 5.5 m tall.
It is some 6,000 years older than Stonehenge.
The site was recognised as prehistoric by the archaeologist Klaus Schmidt in 1994.

q.q: Who built Göbekli Tepe?

catalhoyuk.name: Çatalhöyük
catalhoyuk.t: A Stone Age town with no streets
catalhoyuk.s: On the flat Konya plain stood one of the world's earliest large towns, home to thousands of people more than 9,000 years ago. Its mud-brick houses were packed wall to wall with no streets between them, so people walked across the rooftops and climbed down ladders into their homes. From above, the plain still looks as flat as a table, with the volcano Hasan Dağı rising to the east.
catalhoyuk.w: Look for the vast flat Konya plain, with the lone twin-peaked volcano Hasan Dağı standing to its east.
f: Houses were entered through a hole in the roof.
A wall painting found here may show a town with an erupting volcano behind it.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2012.

q.q: How did people enter houses at Çatalhöyük?

hattusa.name: Hattusa, the Hittite capital
hattusa.t: The land where the Hittite empire rose
hattusa.s: On these bare hills of central Anatolia stood Hattusa, capital of the Hittites, who ruled much of the Bronze Age Near East and dealt as equals with Egypt. Its walls, gates carved with lions and sphinxes, and an archive of clay tablets survive. Among them is one of the oldest peace treaties known. From above, look for the great loop of the Kızılırmak river that wraps around the Hittite heartland.
hattusa.w: Look for the long arc of the Kızılırmak, Turkey's longest river, curving around dry hills east of Ankara.
f: The Hittite king and Egypt's Ramesses II signed a peace treaty around 1259 BC; a copy hangs at UN headquarters.
Hittite is the oldest written Indo-European language known.
Archaeologists have found around 30,000 clay tablets at Hattusa.

q.q: Which pharaoh signed a peace treaty with the Hittites?

petra.name: Petra
petra.t: A city carved into rose-red cliffs
petra.s: In the rugged mountains east of the Wadi Araba lies Petra, capital of the Nabataeans, who grew rich on the incense caravans. They carved temples and tombs straight into the rose-red sandstone and caught every drop of rain in channels and cisterns. You reach its most famous facade, the Treasury, through a narrow gorge. From cruise, look for the jagged, reddish mountain wall above the long, dead-flat rift valley.
petra.w: Look for jagged reddish mountains rising steeply east of the Wadi Araba, the flat rift valley between the Dead Sea and Aqaba.
f: The gorge leading into Petra, the Siq, is about 1.2 km long and in places only a few metres wide.
The Swiss traveller Johann Ludwig Burckhardt brought Petra to Europe's attention in 1812.
A Victorian poem called it 'a rose-red city half as old as time'.

q.q: Who brought Petra to Europe's attention in 1812?

palmyra.name: Palmyra
palmyra.t: The caravan city of the desert palms
palmyra.s: In the middle of the Syrian desert, a spring and a grove of palms made Palmyra a stop for caravans travelling between the Mediterranean and the Euphrates. Its merchants grew so rich that they built a long colonnaded avenue, grand temples and tower tombs, mixing Greek, Roman and Persian styles. From above, look for the green patch of the oasis, sharp against the pale desert around it.
palmyra.w: A small green oasis in a vast pale desert, at the foot of a line of low bare hills.
f: In the 3rd century Queen Zenobia made Palmyra the centre of a short-lived empire.
Palmyrene merchants traded in silk, spices and perfumes from as far as China and India.
The city's own language was a dialect of Aramaic, written in its own script.

q.q: Which queen made Palmyra the heart of an empire?

baalbek.name: Baalbek
baalbek.t: Temples built of some of the largest stones ever moved
baalbek.s: In the Beqaa valley, between two mountain ranges, the Romans built one of their grandest temple complexes, Heliopolis, today's Baalbek. Six towering columns of the Temple of Jupiter still stand, and the Temple of Bacchus beside them is among the best preserved in the Roman world. Its foundations include blocks of hundreds of tonnes each. From above, the long flat valley between two ridges is unmistakable.
baalbek.w: Look for a long, flat green valley running north–south between two parallel mountain ranges, often snow-capped in winter.
f: Three stones in the temple's base, the Trilithon, weigh about 800 tonnes each.
Even larger blocks, never moved, still lie in the ancient quarry nearby.
The Temple of Jupiter's surviving columns are about 20 m tall.

q.q: About how heavy is each stone of Baalbek's Trilithon?

qumran.name: Qumran and the Dead Sea Scrolls
qumran.t: Caves that kept the oldest Bible manuscripts
qumran.s: Look for the Dead Sea, the lowest water on Earth. In 1947 a Bedouin shepherd, searching the cliffs on its north-western shore, found clay jars holding ancient scrolls. Over the next decade the caves around Qumran yielded hundreds of manuscripts, including the oldest known copies of books of the Hebrew Bible. The caves are invisible from here, but the sea and its steep cliffs are striking.
qumran.w: Look for the Dead Sea's long blue northern basin and the steep bare cliffs along its western shore.
f: The scrolls were written roughly between 250 BC and AD 68.
The Great Isaiah Scroll is over 7 m long and nearly complete.
The surface of the Dead Sea lies about 430 m below sea level.

q.q: Who found the first Dead Sea Scrolls in 1947?

babylon.name: Babylon
babylon.t: The ancient world's byword for a great city
babylon.s: On the Euphrates south of Baghdad lie the ruins of Babylon. Under Hammurabi it gave the world one of its first written law codes; under Nebuchadnezzar II it became a city of blue-glazed gates and a towering ziggurat that may lie behind the story of the Tower of Babel. From above, look for the Euphrates and the dark ribbon of palm groves and fields that follows it through the desert.
babylon.w: Look for the Euphrates winding through dry land, lined with dark green palm groves, about 85 km south of Baghdad.
f: Hammurabi's law code, from about 1754 BC, was carved on a black stone stele now in the Louvre.
The blue-tiled Ishtar Gate has been rebuilt in a museum in Berlin.
Babylon became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2019.

q.q: Which king's law code came from Babylon?

ur.name: Ur
ur.t: A Sumerian city still watched over by its ziggurat
ur.s: In the desert of southern Iraq rises the stepped bulk of the Great Ziggurat of Ur, built more than 4,000 years ago. Ur was one of the richest cities of Sumer, a port on the Euphrates close to the Gulf. The river and the coast have since moved away, leaving it stranded in the sand. From cruise the ziggurat is a speck, but the edge of the green river plain against the desert is clear.
ur.w: Look for the boundary between the green Euphrates plain near Nasiriyah and the empty desert just south-west of it.
f: The ziggurat was built by King Ur-Nammu around 2100 BC and partly restored in modern times.
Its royal tombs, dug in the 1920s, held gold helmets, lyres and the mosaic box called the Standard of Ur.
Tradition names 'Ur of the Chaldees' as the birthplace of Abraham.

q.q: Who built the Great Ziggurat of Ur?

uruk.name: Uruk
uruk.t: One of the first cities, where writing began
uruk.s: Here, in what is now desert, stood Uruk, one of the first true cities in the world. By about 3000 BC tens of thousands of people lived inside its walls, and its temple officials began pressing marks into clay tablets to keep accounts: some of the earliest writing anywhere. Legend made Gilgamesh its king. From above, look for the old dry channels of the Euphrates wandering across the plain.
uruk.w: Look for faint old river channels and the edge of green farmland in the desert east of Samawah.
f: The earliest tablets from Uruk, from about 3300 BC, are mostly records of grain, beer and livestock.
Its city walls, credited in legend to Gilgamesh, ran about 9 km around.
The Epic of Gilgamesh is one of the oldest surviving works of literature.

q.q: Which legendary hero was king of Uruk?

nineveh.name: Nineveh
nineveh.t: Assyria's capital and its great library
nineveh.s: On the east bank of the Tigris, opposite Mosul, lie the mounds of Nineveh, once the largest city in the world. Assyrian kings lined its palaces with carved stone reliefs and built canals and aqueducts to water its gardens. King Ashurbanipal gathered a library of clay tablets, and among them was the Epic of Gilgamesh. From above, look for the Tigris flowing south through a city on both banks.
nineveh.w: Look for the Tigris running north–south through the city of Mosul; the ancient mounds lie on its eastern bank.
f: Ashurbanipal's library held tens of thousands of clay tablets, now mostly in the British Museum.
In 1872 a tablet from it was found to tell a flood story much like Noah's.
Sennacherib's canals to Nineveh crossed a valley on the Jerwan aqueduct, one of the oldest known.

q.q: Whose library at Nineveh held the Epic of Gilgamesh?

persepolis.name: Persepolis
persepolis.t: The ceremonial capital of the Persian kings
persepolis.s: On a stone terrace at the foot of a mountain, the Persian kings built Persepolis to receive envoys from across their empire. Its stairways are carved with long processions of Medes, Egyptians, Indians and many others bringing gifts. It was burned in 330 BC after Alexander the Great took it, and its columns still stand among the ruins. From above, look for the wide Marvdasht plain north of Shiraz.
persepolis.w: Look for the broad, farmed Marvdasht plain about 60 km north-east of Shiraz, edged by bare mountains.
f: Darius the Great began building Persepolis around 518 BC.
Its reliefs show envoys of more than 20 peoples bringing gifts to the king.
The tomb of Cyrus the Great stands at nearby Pasargadae.

q.q: Which king founded Persepolis?

yazd.name: Yazd, city of windcatchers
yazd.t: A mud-brick city that learned to live in the desert
yazd.s: Between two great deserts lies Yazd, one of the oldest living cities of Iran. Its old town is built of mud brick, with towers called windcatchers that funnel cool air into the houses below. Water came from qanats, underground channels tunnelled from distant mountains. From cruise, look for a green oasis city on a vast beige plain, with the Shir Kuh mountains to its south-west.
yazd.w: Look for an oasis city on a wide beige desert plain, with the high Shir Kuh mountains to the south-west.
f: The historic city of Yazd became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2017.
A Zoroastrian fire temple in Yazd keeps a flame said to have burned since AD 470.
Qanat shafts show from the air as long dotted lines across the desert, best seen from lower altitude.

q.q: What is a badgir in Yazd?

giza.name: Pyramids of Giza
giza.t: The last Wonder of the ancient world still standing
giza.s: Where the green Nile valley meets the desert, on the western edge of Cairo, stand the pyramids of Giza. The Great Pyramid of Khufu was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for about 3,800 years. Nearby Saqqara holds the step pyramid of Djoser, the first of them all. In clear air, look for three small pale triangles at the desert's edge, right beside the city.
giza.w: Look where Cairo's sprawl meets the desert to the south-west; the pyramids sit on the plateau's edge like pale specks.
f: The Great Pyramid was originally about 146 m tall.
It is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World that still stands.
Its sides face the four compass points with an error of only a fraction of a degree.

q.q: Which pharaoh built the Great Pyramid?

thebes.name: Thebes: Karnak and the Valley of the Kings
thebes.t: Temples on one bank, royal tombs on the other
thebes.s: At Luxor the Nile divides two worlds. On the east bank stood Thebes, capital of Egypt's New Kingdom, with the vast temples of Karnak and Luxor. On the west bank, in desert valleys behind the cliffs, the pharaohs cut their tombs, including Tutankhamun's. From cruise the monuments are too small, but the contrast is striking: a narrow green valley, then sudden bare desert and cliffs.
thebes.w: A thin green strip of fields along the Nile, with the city of Luxor on the east bank and pale cliffs to the west.
f: Karnak is one of the largest religious complexes ever built.
More than 60 tombs have been found in the Valley of the Kings.
Howard Carter found Tutankhamun's nearly intact tomb there in 1922.

q.q: Who found Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922?

abu-simbel.name: Abu Simbel
abu-simbel.t: Temples cut into a mountain, then moved
abu-simbel.s: Look for the huge blue sheet of Lake Nasser in the Nubian desert. On its shore sit the temples of Ramesses II, fronted by four seated giants, each about 20 m tall. When the Aswan High Dam was about to flood them in the 1960s, an international effort led by UNESCO cut the temples into blocks and rebuilt them higher up. The temples are too small to see, but the lake is vast.
abu-simbel.w: A long, branching blue lake in the desert near Egypt's southern border; the temples lie on its western shore.
f: The temples were cut into over 1,000 blocks and rebuilt about 65 m higher.
Twice a year, the rising sun reaches deep inside to light statues in the inner sanctuary.
The rescue campaign helped inspire UNESCO's World Heritage list.

q.q: Why were the Abu Simbel temples moved?
x: To make way for a road

alexandria-ancient.name: Ancient Alexandria
alexandria-ancient.t: The city of the Lighthouse and the Great Library
alexandria-ancient.s: Alexander the Great founded this city on the Mediterranean in 331 BC, and it became the capital of the Ptolemies and the scholarly centre of the ancient world. Its Great Library gathered books from everywhere, and its lighthouse on the island of Pharos was one of the Seven Wonders. From above, look for a long city stretched along the coast between the sea and a lake, west of the Nile delta.
alexandria-ancient.w: A city strung out along the coast for many kilometres, between the sea and Lake Mariout, west of the Nile delta.
f: The Pharos lighthouse stood for centuries; a 15th-century fort now occupies its site.
Eratosthenes estimated the Earth's circumference here around 240 BC, remarkably well.
Cleopatra VII, the last Ptolemaic ruler of Egypt, reigned from Alexandria.

q.q: Who measured the Earth's size from Alexandria?

st-catherine-sinai.name: St Catherine's Monastery, Sinai
st-catherine-sinai.t: A monastery among red granite peaks
st-catherine-sinai.s: In the jagged red granite mountains of southern Sinai, at the foot of the peak tradition calls Mount Sinai, stands St Catherine's Monastery. It was founded in the 6th century and has been lived in by monks ever since, making it one of the oldest working Christian monasteries in the world. Its library holds priceless early manuscripts. From above, look for the wild knot of mountains between two gulfs.
st-catherine-sinai.w: Look for a knot of jagged reddish mountains at the southern tip of Sinai, between the Gulf of Suez and the Gulf of Aqaba.
f: The monastery was built on the orders of Emperor Justinian between about 548 and 565.
The 4th-century Codex Sinaiticus, one of the oldest complete Bibles, was long kept here.
Mount Sinai, the peak above it, rises to about 2,285 m.

q.q: Which emperor founded St Catherine's Monastery?

hegra.name: Hegra (Mada'in Salih)
hegra.t: Petra's southern sister, carved into desert rocks
hegra.s: Among sandstone outcrops that rise like islands from the sand near AlUla lies Hegra, the second city of the Nabataeans after Petra. On the Incense Route, it grew rich from passing caravans, and its people carved more than a hundred monumental tombs into the rocks, many with inscriptions naming their owners. From above, look for wind-sculpted sandstone massifs and the green ribbon of the AlUla oasis.
hegra.w: Look for scattered sandstone outcrops rising from a sandy plain, and the green palm valley of AlUla to the south.
f: Hegra has 111 monumental tombs, 94 of them with decorated facades.
In 2008 it became Saudi Arabia's first UNESCO World Heritage site.
Inscriptions on the tombs record owners' names, dates and fines for anyone who misuses the grave.

q.q: Which people carved the tombs of Hegra?

marib.name: Marib, the land of Sheba
marib.t: Capital of Saba and its famous dam
marib.s: Where the mountains of Yemen meet the desert stood Marib, capital of the kingdom of Saba, the biblical Sheba. Its wealth came from incense and from a great dam that stored the seasonal floods and watered a huge oasis. For more than a thousand years it was one of the engineering wonders of Arabia. From above, look for the line where dark highlands give way to open sand.
marib.w: Look where the dark Yemeni highlands end abruptly at the edge of the sandy Ramlat al-Sab'atayn desert.
f: The Great Dam of Marib was about 600 m long and fed canals that watered thousands of hectares.
Tradition links the kingdom of Saba with the Queen of Sheba.
In 2023 UNESCO listed Marib's ancient sites as World Heritage.

q.q: Which legendary queen is linked with Saba?

dilmun.name: Dilmun burial mounds
dilmun.t: The Bronze Age trading island of the Gulf
dilmun.s: Bahrain was the heart of Dilmun, a Bronze Age trading power that linked Mesopotamia with the Indus valley. Sumerian poems describe it as a pure land of fresh water. Its people built tens of thousands of burial mounds, which once covered much of the island. They are too small to see from cruise, but the island itself is clear, tied to Arabia by a long causeway.
dilmun.w: Look for a low sandy island in the Gulf, joined to the Saudi coast by a long causeway to its west.
f: Around 11,000 of the burial mounds survive, and many more once existed.
Dilmun's ships carried copper from Oman to the cities of Mesopotamia.
The mounds became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2019.

q.q: Which modern country was the heart of Dilmun?

mesopotamia.name: Mesopotamia
mesopotamia.t: The land between the rivers, where cities began
mesopotamia.s: This is the land between the Tigris and the Euphrates, where people first built cities, wrote on clay and kept laws in writing. Sumer, Akkad, Assyria and Babylon all rose here, fed by irrigation canals in a land of little rain. From cruise you can see why it mattered: two green river ribbons crossing an otherwise brown plain, converging towards the Gulf.
mesopotamia.w: Look for two rivers, each lined with green, running south-east across a brown plain and slowly converging.
f: Our 60-minute hour and 360-degree circle come from Mesopotamian counting in sixties.
The name is Greek for 'between the rivers'.
The Tigris and Euphrates finally join to form the Shatt al-Arab before reaching the Gulf.

q.q: What does the name 'Mesopotamia' mean?

cappadocia.name: Cappadocia
cappadocia.t: A land carved from volcanic ash
cappadocia.s: Ancient eruptions buried this part of Anatolia in thick volcanic ash, which hardened into soft rock. Wind and rain carved it into cones and pillars, and people carved it too: cave houses, rock-cut churches painted with frescoes, and whole underground towns many levels deep. From cruise the fairy chimneys are invisible, but the snow-capped volcano Erciyes that helped make them is a landmark.
cappadocia.w: Look for the big snowy cone of Mount Erciyes near Kayseri; the rock valleys lie about 70 km west of it.
f: The underground city of Derinkuyu reaches about 85 m below ground.
Göreme's rock-cut churches hold frescoes painted between the 10th and 12th centuries.
Cappadocia became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1985.

q.q: What formed Cappadocia's soft rock?

lycia.name: Lycia
lycia.t: Temple-fronted tombs cut into seaside cliffs
lycia.s: Where the Taurus mountains plunge into the turquoise Mediterranean lay Lycia, a land of proud city-states. Its people cut tombs into cliff faces with fronts like little temples, and they joined in a league that gave larger cities more votes. Today the same coast is a holiday favourite. From above, look for the rugged peninsula between Fethiye and Antalya, its mountains falling straight into the sea.
lycia.w: Look for a mountainous peninsula jutting into the sea between the bays of Fethiye and Antalya.
f: The Lycian League was praised by Montesquieu and cited in the Federalist Papers.
St Nicholas, the model for Santa Claus, was bishop of the Lycian city of Myra.
The Lycian Way, a hiking trail of more than 500 km, links many of the ancient sites.

q.q: Which saint was bishop of Myra in Lycia?

phoenicia.name: Phoenicia
phoenicia.t: The seafarers who gave the world an alphabet
phoenicia.s: On this narrow strip between the mountains of Lebanon and the sea lived the Phoenicians, the great sailors of the ancient Mediterranean. From Tyre, Sidon and Byblos they traded cedar wood and purple cloth, founded Carthage and settlements as far as Spain. Their simple alphabet of 22 letters spread with them and became the ancestor of Greek, Latin and many others. The coast and its snowy mountains are easy to see.
phoenicia.w: Look for a thin coastal strip of towns backed by a high mountain range, often snowy in winter and spring.
f: Tyrian purple dye was made from sea snails and was worth more than its weight in gold.
The word 'Bible' comes via Greek from the Phoenician port of Byblos.
The Phoenician alphabet had 22 letters, all of them consonants.

q.q: What is the Phoenicians' most lasting gift?

mesopotamian-marshes.name: Mesopotamian Marshes
mesopotamian-marshes.t: Reed villages that Sumer would recognise
mesopotamian-marshes.s: Where the Tigris and Euphrates approach each other near the Gulf, they spread into a vast maze of lakes and reed beds. For thousands of years the Marsh Arabs have lived here, building arched houses entirely of reeds and herding water buffalo by boat. Carvings from Sumer show almost identical buildings. From above, look for a patchwork of blue water and green-brown reeds in the desert.
mesopotamian-marshes.w: A mosaic of lakes, channels and reed beds, blue and green against the desert, between Nasiriyah and Basra.
f: The marshes became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2016.
Traditional guest houses called mudhif are built of reeds without a single nail.
Some writers have linked the marshes with the biblical Garden of Eden.

q.q: What is a traditional mudhif built from?

faiyum.name: Faiyum oasis
faiyum.t: A green fan in the desert, watered by the Nile
faiyum.s: South-west of Cairo, a desert basin is fed by a canal from the Nile, turning it into a green fan of fields around a salty lake. Pharaohs of the Middle Kingdom developed it for farming almost 4,000 years ago, and in Roman times its people were buried with lifelike painted portraits. From cruise it is one of Egypt's clearest sights: a bright green patch alone in the desert.
faiyum.w: A bright green fan-shaped oasis in the desert west of the Nile, with a long lake along its northern edge.
f: The Faiyum mummy portraits, painted on wood, are among the finest portraits to survive from antiquity.
Nearby Wadi Al-Hitan holds fossils of ancient whales that once swam in a sea here.
Lake Qarun, on the oasis's northern edge, lies below sea level.

q.q: What are the famous Roman-era finds of the Faiyum?

silk-road-northern.name: Silk Road (northern route)
silk-road-northern.t: The caravan road that tied China to the Mediterranean
silk-road-northern.s: This was the main artery of the Silk Road, from Chang'an in China through the Hexi Corridor and the Tarim oases to Samarkand, Persia and the Mediterranean. Silk went west; horses, glass, spices and ideas travelled in every direction, and Buddhism reached China this way. No caravan went end to end. From above, look for oasis towns strung like beads between snowy mountains and desert.
silk-road-northern.w: Look for green oases strung along the foot of snowy mountains, with sand or gravel desert on the other side.
f: The name 'Silk Road' was coined in 1877 by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen.
Paper-making travelled west along these routes from China.
In 2014 the section from Chang'an to the Tian Shan became a UNESCO World Heritage site.

q.q: Who coined the term 'Silk Road' in 1877?

silk-road-southern.name: Silk Road (southern Tarim route)
silk-road-southern.t: Oasis to oasis between desert and the Kunlun
silk-road-southern.s: This branch of the Silk Road skirted the southern edge of the Taklamakan desert, hopping from oasis to oasis along streams that run down from the Kunlun mountains. Khotan, its jewel, was famous for jade and for Buddhist learning. From Kashgar and Tashkurgan caravans climbed over the Pamirs towards Afghanistan. From cruise it is spectacular: a wall of snowy peaks on one side, a sea of dunes on the other.
silk-road-southern.w: Look for a line of small green oases between the snowy Kunlun range to the south and the Taklamakan's dunes to the north.
f: Khotan's jade was carried east to China for thousands of years.
Legend says silkworm eggs were smuggled to Khotan hidden in a princess's headdress.
The monk Xuanzang took this route home from India, reaching Chang'an in 645.

q.q: Which precious stone made Khotan famous?

silk-road-tianshan.name: Silk Road (Tian Shan corridor)
silk-road-tianshan.t: Along the northern foot of the Heavenly Mountains
silk-road-tianshan.s: North of the Tian Shan, the Heavenly Mountains, another branch of the Silk Road ran from Turpan past today's Ürümqi and Almaty to the cities of the Syr Darya. It passed through well-watered valleys and grassland, good country for horses and for nomads who traded with the caravans. From cruise, follow the long snowy wall of the Tian Shan with green foothills and cities at its feet.
silk-road-tianshan.w: Follow the long snowy wall of the Tian Shan, with cities and green foothills along its northern base.
f: The Tang poet Li Bai is often said to have been born near Suyab, a city on this route.
Otrar, near its western end, was the birthplace of the philosopher al-Farabi.
The route passes Sayram Lake, a blue alpine lake high in the mountains.

q.q: Which mountain lake lies on this route?

maritime-silk-road.name: Maritime Silk Road
maritime-silk-road.t: The monsoon highway from China to the Gulf
maritime-silk-road.s: Long before planes, the sea linked Asia. Ships carried silk, porcelain and tea from southern China through the Strait of Malacca and across the Indian Ocean to India, Arabia and East Africa, returning with spices, ivory and incense. Sailors timed their voyages to the monsoon winds, which reverse each season. Look for the island-studded coasts and straits where ports grew rich on this trade.
maritime-silk-road.w: Look for busy straits and island coasts, especially the narrow Strait of Malacca between Malaysia and Sumatra.
f: The Ming admiral Zheng He led seven great fleets across the Indian Ocean between 1405 and 1433.
Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta both described Quanzhou as one of the world's greatest ports.
A 9th-century Arab ship found off Indonesia carried about 60,000 pieces of Chinese pottery.

q.q: Which Ming admiral led fleets across the Indian Ocean?

trans-caspian-railway.name: Trans-Caspian Railway
trans-caspian-railway.t: The first railway across Central Asia's deserts
trans-caspian-railway.s: This is the first railway of Central Asia. The Russian Empire began it on the Caspian shore in 1880 and pushed it east along the foot of the Kopet Dag mountains, across the Karakum desert and over the Amu Darya to Bukhara and Samarkand. Travellers could now reach the Silk Road cities by train. Look for the green strip at the mountains' foot and the empty desert beyond.
trans-caspian-railway.w: Look for the Kopet Dag range with a strip of green towns along its northern foot, and the Karakum sands beyond.
f: It was the first railway built in Central Asia.
The line reached Samarkand in 1888 and Tashkent in 1898.
