It was built under the direction of General Mikhail Annenkov.

q.q: Which desert did the Trans-Caspian Railway cross?

samarkand.name: Samarkand
samarkand.t: The blue-domed crossroads of the Silk Road
samarkand.s: Samarkand is more than 2,500 years old and was for centuries the great meeting point of the Silk Road. Under Timur and his descendants in the 14th and 15th centuries it was filled with turquoise domes and tiled madrasas, and its Registan square is still one of the grandest in the Islamic world. From above, look for the city spread across the green Zeravshan valley, with mountains rising to the south.
samarkand.w: Look for a large city in the green, irrigated Zeravshan valley, with mountain ridges to the south and desert beyond.
f: The ruler Ulugh Beg built an observatory here in the 1420s and catalogued about a thousand stars.
Samarkand paper was famous across the Islamic world from the 8th century.
The city became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2001.

q.q: Which ruler built an observatory in Samarkand?

bukhara.name: Bukhara
bukhara.t: A holy city of scholars, domes and bazaars
bukhara.s: In an oasis at the end of the Zeravshan river lies Bukhara, one of the best-preserved medieval cities of Central Asia. In the 9th and 10th centuries it was the capital of the Samanids and a centre of Persian poetry and science. Its old centre still has covered bazaars, madrasas and a 12th-century minaret. From above, look for a green oasis surrounded by desert, west of Samarkand.
bukhara.w: Look for a green irrigated oasis ringed by desert, about 220 km west of Samarkand.
f: The physician and philosopher Avicenna was born near Bukhara in 980.
The Kalyan Minaret, built in 1127, rises about 46 m above the old town.
The Samanid Mausoleum, from the 10th century, is a masterpiece of decorative brickwork.

q.q: Which great physician was born near Bukhara?

khiva.name: Khiva
khiva.t: A walled desert town like a museum under open sky
khiva.s: On the edge of the Karakum desert, in the delta oasis of the Amu Darya, stands Khiva. Its inner town, Itchan Kala, is enclosed by mud-brick walls and crammed with minarets, madrasas and palaces, mostly from the 18th and 19th centuries. It was the last stop before caravans crossed the desert to Persia. From above, look for the green irrigated oasis sharp against sand on every side.
khiva.w: Look for a large green irrigated oasis on the Amu Darya, with bare desert pressing in on all sides.
f: Itchan Kala became Uzbekistan's first UNESCO World Heritage site in 1990.
The Kalta Minor minaret was left unfinished and stands short and wide, covered in turquoise tiles.
The mathematician al-Khwarizmi, whose name gave us the word 'algorithm', came from this region.

q.q: Which word comes from the name of Khwarazm's mathematician?

merv.name: Merv
merv.t: Once one of the largest cities in the world
merv.s: In the delta of the Murghab river, in the Karakum desert, lie the ruins of Merv. For 2,000 years a succession of walled cities rose side by side here, each built next to the last. In the 12th century, as capital of the Seljuk sultans, it was among the largest cities on Earth. From above, look for the green oasis of Mary amid the desert; the ruins lie just east of the town.
merv.w: Look for the green delta oasis of the Murghab river in the Karakum; the ruins lie just east of the city of Mary.
f: The mausoleum of Sultan Sanjar, from the 12th century, still has its great brick dome.
Its oldest walled city, Erk Kala, dates to the Achaemenid Persian era.
Ancient Merv became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1999.

q.q: In which river's delta did Merv grow?

ani.name: Ani
ani.t: The medieval city of a thousand and one churches
ani.s: On a triangle of plateau above a river gorge stand the ruins of Ani, capital of a medieval Armenian kingdom. In the 11th century it was one of the great cities of its age, its skyline crowded with churches. Many still stand, roofless, on the open grassland. From above, look for the high plateau and the deep gorge that today marks the border between Turkey and Armenia.
ani.w: Look for a high green-brown plateau cut by a deep river gorge, east of the town of Kars.
f: Ani was nicknamed 'the city of 1,001 churches'.
Its cathedral, finished around 1001, uses pointed arches long before Gothic Europe.
Ani became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2016.

q.q: What was Ani's nickname?

mtskheta.name: Mtskheta
mtskheta.t: Georgia's ancient capital where two rivers meet
mtskheta.s: Just north of Tbilisi, where the Aragvi flows into the Kura, lies Mtskheta, the ancient capital of the Georgian kingdom of Iberia. Here Georgia adopted Christianity in the 4th century, one of the first countries to do so. A small 6th-century monastery, Jvari, watches over the confluence from a hilltop. From above, look for the two rivers meeting in a green valley, often in two different colours.
mtskheta.w: Look for two rivers joining in a narrow green valley about 20 km north of Tbilisi.
f: Svetitskhoveli Cathedral in Mtskheta was built in the 11th century on an older church site.
Jvari Monastery gave its name to a whole style of Georgian church architecture.
Mtskheta's churches became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1994.

q.q: Which two rivers meet at Mtskheta?

derbent.name: Derbent
derbent.t: The Gate of Gates between mountains and sea
derbent.s: Here the Caucasus mountains come within a few kilometres of the Caspian Sea, leaving a narrow pass along the coast. In the 6th century Persian kings built two parallel stone walls from the mountain fortress down into the sea to control it. Arab geographers called it the Gate of Gates. From above, the reason is obvious: a thin coastal strip squeezed between blue water and steep ridges.
derbent.w: Look for a narrow coastal plain squeezed between the Caspian Sea and the steep foothills of the Caucasus.
f: Derbent is often called the oldest city in Russia.
Its walls once ran out into the sea, forming a guarded harbour.
The citadel and old city became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2003.

q.q: Which sea do Derbent's walls run down to?

baikonur.name: Baikonur, launch site of the first human spaceflight
baikonur.t: Where the first human left for space
baikonur.s: On the flat steppe of Kazakhstan, near the Syr Darya river, lies the world's first spaceport. The first artificial satellite, Sputnik, was launched from here in 1957. On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin lifted off from the same pad to become the first human in space. From above, look for the ribbon of the Syr Darya across the dry steppe, and the town of Baikonur beside it.
baikonur.w: Look for the thin green ribbon of the Syr Darya crossing flat, dry steppe, with a town and scattered launch complexes north of it.
f: Gagarin's flight lasted 108 minutes and made one orbit of the Earth.
His launch pad, known as Gagarin's Start, stayed in use for more than 60 years.
The cosmodrome is leased by Russia from Kazakhstan.

q.q: How long did Gagarin's first spaceflight last?

arkaim.name: Arkaim
arkaim.t: A ring-shaped Bronze Age town in the Ural steppe
arkaim.s: On the open steppe east of the southern Urals lie the remains of Arkaim, a fortified settlement built around 4,000 years ago as two rings of walls with houses set against them. It belongs to the Sintashta culture, known for some of the world's earliest spoked-wheel chariots. The rings are too faint to see from cruise, but the rolling grassland around them has changed little since.
arkaim.w: Look for open, rolling steppe with river valleys and few trees, south of Chelyabinsk and east of the Ural ridges.
f: Arkaim was found in 1987 by archaeologists surveying land for a planned reservoir.
The discovery led to the reservoir plan being dropped and the land becoming a reserve.
The settlement was about 150 m across.

q.q: What nearly flooded Arkaim soon after it was found?

khorezm.name: Khwarazm
khorezm.t: An oasis kingdom on the Amu Darya delta
khorezm.s: Where the Amu Darya fans out before the Aral Sea, irrigation created a green island between two deserts: Khwarazm, home to kingdoms for 2,500 years. Dozens of ancient mud-brick fortresses still stand on the desert edge, and its old capital, Konye-Urgench, keeps a soaring minaret. From cruise the oasis is one of the region's clearest sights: a big patch of green and water in beige desert.
khorezm.w: A large green patchwork of irrigated fields and canals on the lower Amu Darya, between the Karakum and Kyzylkum deserts.
f: The scholar al-Biruni, born here in 973, calculated the Earth's radius with remarkable accuracy.
The Kutlug Timur minaret in Konye-Urgench is about 60 m tall.
The fortresses of ancient Khwarazm are among the oldest in Central Asia.

q.q: Which scholar born in Khwarazm measured the Earth's radius?

bactria.name: Bactria
bactria.t: Where Greek, Persian and Indian worlds met
bactria.s: Between the Hindu Kush and the Amu Darya lay Bactria, a rich land of oasis cities. It was a Persian province, then a Greek kingdom founded by Alexander's successors, then the heart of the Kushan empire, which carried Buddhism north along the Silk Road. Its chief city, Balkh, was called the mother of cities. From above, look for the Amu Darya's green valley with the Hindu Kush to the south.
bactria.w: Look for the green valley of the Amu Darya, with the high, often snowy Hindu Kush rising to the south.
f: A Greek city with a theatre and gymnasium, Ai-Khanoum, stood on the Amu Darya in the 3rd century BC.
The two-humped Bactrian camel is named after this region.
The poet Rumi is known in Persian as Balkhi, 'from Balkh'.

q.q: What was Balkh called in ancient times?

scythian-steppe.name: Scythian steppe
scythian-steppe.t: Grasslands of the nomads and their golden kurgans
scythian-steppe.s: North of the Black Sea stretches the steppe where the Scythians once lived: horse-riding nomads who moved with their herds and buried their leaders under great earth mounds called kurgans. Their goldsmiths made some of the finest animal-style jewellery of the ancient world. Today the land is farmed in huge fields, and from above it looks like a patchwork quilt on a flat table.
scythian-steppe.w: A vast flat plain of large rectangular fields, cut by broad rivers flowing south to the Black Sea.
f: Herodotus devoted a whole book of his Histories to the Scythians.
A gold pectoral found in a kurgan in 1971 is one of the masterpieces of Scythian art.
Kurgans still rise from the fields, some nearly 20 m high.

q.q: Which Greek historian described the Scythians?

colchis.name: Colchis
colchis.t: The land of the Golden Fleece
colchis.s: Between the Caucasus and the Black Sea lies the green, humid lowland of Colchis, in today's western Georgia. Greek myth sent Jason and the Argonauts here to seize the Golden Fleece. Historians note that people in the nearby mountains once caught gold dust from rivers on sheepskins, which may lie behind the legend. From above, look for the flat green plain of the Rioni river opening to the sea.
colchis.w: Look for a flat, very green lowland along the eastern Black Sea, where the Rioni river reaches the coast at Poti.
f: Excavations at Vani have uncovered rich gold jewellery made in Colchis.
The region is one of the wettest in the Caucasus, which keeps it green all year.
Greek colonists founded trading towns on the Colchian coast from the 6th century BC.

q.q: What did Jason seek in Colchis?

urartu.name: Urartu
urartu.t: The Iron Age kingdom of Lake Van and Ararat
urartu.s: Around the vast blue Lake Van lay Urartu, a mountain kingdom of the Iron Age. Its kings built fortresses on rocky crags, cut irrigation canals through the valleys and left inscriptions in cuneiform. Its name survives in Ararat, the snow-capped volcano on its northern edge. From cruise this is superb country: a huge lake, volcano cones and high, bare plateaus.
urartu.w: Look for the huge blue Lake Van, and to its north-east the lone white cone of Mount Ararat.
f: Yerevan grew from the Urartian fortress of Erebuni, founded in 782 BC.
A canal built by King Menua in the 8th century BC still carries water to the Van area.
Lake Van is a salty soda lake where only one kind of fish can live.

q.q: Which city grew from the fortress of Erebuni?

volga-trade-route.name: Volga trade route
volga-trade-route.t: Viking traders on Europe's longest river
volga-trade-route.s: In the Viking Age, traders from Scandinavia rowed their boats down the Volga to the markets of Bulgar and the Caspian, exchanging furs, wax and honey for Arab silver. Some went on to Baghdad. The river still shows the way: follow its wide blue course, now broken by long reservoirs, as it curves south across Russia towards the Caspian.
volga-trade-route.w: Follow the Volga, broad and blue with long reservoirs, curving south towards the Caspian lowlands.
f: Tens of thousands of Arab silver coins have been found in Viking-age hoards in Scandinavia.
In 922 the Arab envoy Ibn Fadlan described meeting Rus traders on the Volga.
The Volga is Europe's longest river, about 3,500 km.

q.q: What coins flowed north along the Volga route?

varangians-to-greeks.name: Route from the Varangians to the Greeks
varangians-to-greeks.t: The river road from the Baltic to Constantinople
varangians-to-greeks.s: Here ran the great river road of early Rus, from the Baltic to Constantinople. Traders and travellers sailed up the Volkhov through Novgorod to Lake Ilmen, dragged their boats overland between rivers, then floated down the Dnieper past Kyiv to the Black Sea. The route helped bind the first East Slavic state together. From above, follow the chain of lakes and the broad Dnieper as it runs south.
varangians-to-greeks.w: Look for Lake Ilmen and the Volkhov in the north, and far to the south the broad Dnieper flowing to the Black Sea.
f: The route is described in the Primary Chronicle, written in Kyiv in the early 12th century.
Where rivers did not connect, boats were hauled overland on rollers along portages.
A 10th-century Byzantine emperor recorded the names of the Dnieper rapids in two languages, Slavic and Norse.

q.q: Which chronicle describes this route?

trans-siberian-railway.name: Trans-Siberian Railway
trans-siberian-railway.t: The longest railway on Earth, Moscow to the Pacific
trans-siberian-railway.s: This is the longest railway line in the world, about 9,300 km from Moscow to Vladivostok. Built between 1891 and 1916, it tied Siberia and the Pacific coast to European Russia and turned a journey of months into one of days. From cruise, look for towns strung along a line through endless taiga, and for its great bridges over the Ob, the Yenisei and the Amur.
trans-siberian-railway.w: Look for a chain of towns and clearings along a line through dark forest, crossing great rivers on long bridges.
f: Construction was formally begun in Vladivostok in May 1891 by the future Tsar Nicholas II.
The line along the southern shore of Lake Baikal has dozens of tunnels cut into the cliffs.
The full journey by train takes about a week and crosses seven time-zone changes.

q.q: Where was construction formally begun in 1891?

chinese-eastern-railway.name: Chinese Eastern Railway
chinese-eastern-railway.s: Instead of following the long Amur bend, Russia built a shortcut straight across Manchuria to Vladivostok between 1897 and 1903. The line crossed the Greater Khingan mountains and the wide Manchurian plain, and at its junction on the Songhua river a new city grew: Harbin. From above, look for the forested Khingan ridges giving way to a vast flat farmland plain.
chinese-eastern-railway.w: Look for forested Greater Khingan ridges in the west, then a vast, flat patchwork of farmland around Harbin.
f: Harbin was founded in 1898 as the railway's hub.
Harbin's old centre still has streets of Russian-style buildings from the railway era.
The line crossed the Greater Khingan through a tunnel about 3 km long.

q.q: Which city grew up as the railway's hub in 1898?

siberian-trakt.name: Great Siberian Road (Siberian Trakt)
siberian-trakt.t: The post road across Siberia before the railway
siberian-trakt.s: Before the railway, this was the road to Siberia. From the 18th century the Siberian Trakt ran from Moscow over the Urals, through Tyumen, Tomsk and Irkutsk to Kyakhta on the Chinese border. Mail coaches, tea caravans and settlers used it, changing horses at post stations. The modern highway and railway follow much of its line through birch forest and taiga, still visible as a thin thread.
siberian-trakt.w: Look for a road and railway threading east through birch forest and taiga, linking towns on the big rivers.
f: Anton Chekhov travelled it in 1890 on his way to Sakhalin and wrote about its mud and its people.
Tea from China came west along the road from Kyakhta.
It was one of the longest roads in the world when it was completed.

q.q: Which writer crossed Siberia on this road in 1890?

great-tea-road.name: Great Tea Road
great-tea-road.t: Tea by camel from China to Russia
great-tea-road.s: For about two centuries, tea from the hills of southern China travelled north by river boat, cart and camel caravan across the Gobi and the Mongolian steppe to the border town of Kyakhta. There it was traded for furs and cloth and carried on across Siberia to Moscow. From above, look for the vast empty Gobi and the green valleys of the Selenga north of Ulaanbaatar.
great-tea-road.w: Look for the pale, empty Gobi giving way to the green Mongolian steppe and river valleys near Ulaanbaatar.
f: A treaty in 1727 made Kyakhta the official place of trade between Russia and China.
Pressed tea bricks were used as money on the steppe.
Kyakhta's merchants became some of the richest people in the Russian Empire.

q.q: Which border town was the hub of the tea trade?

veliky-novgorod.name: Veliky Novgorod
veliky-novgorod.t: A medieval merchant republic that wrote on birch bark
veliky-novgorod.s: On the Volkhov river, just north of Lake Ilmen, stands Novgorod, one of the oldest cities of Russia. For more than three centuries it was a merchant republic whose town assembly, the veche, chose its princes. Its soggy soil preserved over a thousand letters scratched on birch bark by ordinary people. From above, look for the lake and the river flowing north out of it through the city.
veliky-novgorod.w: Look for Lake Ilmen, with the Volkhov river flowing north out of it through the city.
f: The first birch-bark letter was found here in 1951; more turn up every year.
St Sophia Cathedral, built in 1045–1050, is one of the oldest churches in Russia.
Novgorod's monuments became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1992.

q.q: What did archaeologists find in Novgorod in 1951?

staraya-ladoga.name: Staraya Ladoga
staraya-ladoga.t: Where the story of Rus begins
staraya-ladoga.s: Just before the Volkhov river enters Lake Ladoga lies Staraya Ladoga, a village that was once a busy trading town of Scandinavians, Slavs and Finns. Tree-ring dating puts its first buildings in the mid-8th century, making it one of the oldest towns of Rus. Chronicles link it with Rurik, the legendary founder of the first princely dynasty. From above, look for the Volkhov's final stretch and Europe's largest lake.
staraya-ladoga.w: Look for the Volkhov river running north into the south shore of the huge Lake Ladoga.
f: Its earliest timber buildings have been dated by their tree rings to around 753.
Lake Ladoga, just to the north, is the largest lake in Europe.
The stone fortress by the river dates from the 12th and 16th centuries.

q.q: Which lake lies just north of Staraya Ladoga?

kizhi.name: Kizhi Pogost
kizhi.t: Twenty-two wooden domes on a northern island
kizhi.s: On a small island in Lake Onega stands one of the wonders of wooden architecture: the Church of the Transfiguration, built in 1714, with 22 onion domes covered in silvery aspen shingles. Beside it rise a smaller church and a bell tower. Legend says the master builder threw his axe into the lake when he finished. From above, look for Lake Onega's northern bays, scattered with long narrow islands.
kizhi.w: Look for the northern part of Lake Onega, a maze of long, narrow islands and bays in the Karelian forest.
f: The Church of the Transfiguration is about 37 m tall and built entirely of wood.
Its neighbour, the Church of the Intercession, has nine domes.
Kizhi Pogost became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1990.

q.q: How many domes crown the Church of the Transfiguration?

solovki.name: Solovetsky Islands
solovki.t: A fortress monastery on the White Sea
solovki.s: Far out in the White Sea, just below the Arctic Circle, lie the Solovetsky Islands. Monks founded a monastery here in the 15th century, and it grew into a fortress of huge boulders, a trading power and a centre of northern culture. The islands also hold ancient stone labyrinths laid out by earlier peoples. From above, look for a cluster of forested islands dotted with lakes in the open sea.
solovki.w: Look for a cluster of low, forested islands full of small lakes, in the western part of the White Sea.
f: The monastery walls are built of boulders, some weighing several tonnes.
The monks dug canals linking dozens of the island's lakes.
The islands' monuments became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1992.

q.q: Which sea surrounds the Solovetsky Islands?

bolghar.name: Bolghar
bolghar.t: The northern trading capital on the Volga
bolghar.s: Near where the Kama joins the Volga stood Bolghar, capital of Volga Bulgaria and one of the great markets of medieval Eurasia. Furs from the northern forests met silver and silks from the south. In 922 its ruler received an embassy from the Caliph of Baghdad and officially adopted Islam. From above, look for the vast Kuybyshev Reservoir, where two great rivers meet.
bolghar.w: Look for the enormous Kuybyshev Reservoir where the Kama joins the Volga, south of Kazan.
f: The Arab envoy Ibn Fadlan wrote a vivid account of his journey here in 922.
Bolghar became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2014.
The Kuybyshev Reservoir beside it is the largest reservoir in Europe.

q.q: In which year did Volga Bulgaria adopt Islam?

tobolsk.name: Tobolsk
tobolsk.s: Where the Tobol flows into the Irtysh, Russian settlers founded Tobolsk in 1587, and for about two centuries it was the capital of all Siberia. On a high bluff above the rivers stands the only stone kremlin in Siberia, with white walls and church domes. The cartographer Semyon Remezov, who helped build it, also drew the first atlas of Siberia. From above, look for two rivers meeting in the taiga.
tobolsk.w: Look for the meeting of the Tobol and the Irtysh, with the old town on a high bluff above the floodplain.
f: The chemist Dmitri Mendeleev was born in Tobolsk in 1834.
Its kremlin was built of stone around 1700.
Tobolsk was the starting point for many expeditions further east.

q.q: Which scientist was born in Tobolsk?

mangazeya.name: Mangazeya
mangazeya.t: A lost Arctic boomtown of the fur trade
mangazeya.s: In the tundra on the Taz river, above the Arctic Circle, stood Mangazeya, the first Russian town in the Siberian Arctic. For a few decades in the 17th century it boomed on sable furs, reached by sea from the White Sea and by river. Then trade moved away and the town was abandoned. From above, look for the Taz winding through flat, lake-speckled tundra towards the Gulf of Ob.
mangazeya.w: Look for the Taz river winding through flat tundra full of lakes, east of the long Gulf of Ob.
f: Contemporaries called it 'gold-seething Mangazeya' for its riches.
In 1619 the tsar banned the sea route there, fearing foreign ships would follow it.
Excavations have found leather shoes, chess pieces and seals from across Europe.

q.q: What made Mangazeya rich?

gagarin-landing.name: Gagarin's landing site
gagarin-landing.t: Where the first spaceman came back to Earth
gagarin-landing.s: On the morning of 12 April 1961, after one orbit of the Earth, Yuri Gagarin came down by parachute in a field on the Volga steppe, near the city of Engels. As planned, he had ejected from his capsule, which landed separately nearby. The first people he met were a forester's wife and her granddaughter. From above, look for the wide Volga at Saratov, with Engels on its eastern bank.
gagarin-landing.w: Look for the broad Volga at Saratov; the landing site lies in the steppe a little south of Engels on the east bank.
f: Gagarin landed about 108 minutes after launch.
The site is now a memorial park with a tall monument.
Vostok 1 was designed so that the pilot landed apart from the capsule by parachute.

q.q: How did Gagarin land?
q.a: By parachute, apart from the capsule

golden-ring.name: Golden Ring of Russia
golden-ring.t: Old Russian towns of white stone and onion domes
golden-ring.s: North-east of Moscow lies a loop of old towns: Vladimir, Suzdal, Rostov, Yaroslavl, Kostroma and others. Between the 12th and 17th centuries they were princely capitals and monastery centres, and their white-stone churches, kremlins and onion domes still stand among fields and forests. From above, look for the Volga and for round Lake Pleshcheyevo and Lake Nero among the woods.
golden-ring.w: Look for the Volga at Yaroslavl, and smaller round lakes, Pleshcheyevo and Nero, among forest and fields to the south.
f: The name 'Golden Ring' was coined by a journalist in 1967.
The white-stone monuments of Vladimir and Suzdal became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1992.
The Church of the Intercession on the Nerl, from 1165, stands alone in a water meadow.

q.q: When was the name 'Golden Ring' coined?

grand-trunk-road.name: Grand Trunk Road
grand-trunk-road.t: Two thousand years of traffic across the Ganges plain
grand-trunk-road.s: This is one of Asia's oldest and longest roads, crossing the Indo-Gangetic plain from Bengal to Kabul, some 2,500 km. It follows an ancient route, but the 16th-century ruler Sher Shah Suri rebuilt it with rest houses, wells and shade trees. Rudyard Kipling called it a river of life. From cruise, look for the flat green plain with the Ganges and cities strung along the line.
grand-trunk-road.w: Look for the vast flat green plain of northern India, with the Ganges and a line of big cities running north-west.
f: Sher Shah Suri marked distances along it with pillars called kos minars, some still standing.
The road crosses the Khyber Pass on its way to Kabul.
Much of it is still a main highway, now national roads in several countries.

q.q: Which 16th-century ruler rebuilt the Grand Trunk Road?

grand-canal.name: Grand Canal of China
grand-canal.t: The world's longest canal, Beijing to Hangzhou
grand-canal.s: For more than a thousand years this canal carried rice from the fertile south to feed the capital in the north. Begun in pieces as early as the 5th century BC and joined into one system in the early 7th, it runs about 1,800 km from Hangzhou to Beijing, crossing the Yangtze and the Yellow River. In the south it is still busy with barges, and in clear weather its line can be traced.
grand-canal.w: Between Hangzhou and Yangzhou, look for a waterway threading past Suzhou and Wuxi among lakes and fields.
f: It is the longest artificial waterway in the world.
The pound lock, with gates at both ends, was invented in China in the 10th century for canals like this.
The Grand Canal became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2014.

q.q: Which two cities does the Grand Canal link?

great-wall.name: Great Wall of China
great-wall.t: Two thousand years of walls across mountains and desert
great-wall.s: Chinese states and dynasties built walls along their northern frontier for about 2,000 years, and the stone-and-brick wall most people picture was raised by the Ming after 1368. It runs from the Gobi at Jiayuguan to the sea at Shanhaiguan, riding mountain ridges. It is only a few metres wide, so it cannot be seen from cruise height, but the ridges and deserts it crossed are easy to see.
great-wall.w: North of Beijing, look for steep, wrinkled mountain ridges; far to the west, the gravel desert of the Hexi Corridor.
f: A 2012 survey measured all sections built over the centuries at about 21,000 km.
The idea that the wall is visible from the Moon is a myth.
At Old Dragon's Head near Shanhaiguan the wall runs down into the sea.

q.q: How long are all sections of the Great Wall combined?

tea-horse-road.name: Tea Horse Road
tea-horse-road.t: Tea from Yunnan carried over mountains to Tibet
tea-horse-road.s: For more than a thousand years, caravans of mules and porters carried bricks of tea from Yunnan and Sichuan up into Tibet, and brought back horses. The road climbed through some of the deepest gorges on Earth, where the Yangtze, the Mekong and the Salween run side by side, and over passes above 4,000 m. From cruise the land is breathtaking: parallel river canyons and snowy peaks.
tea-horse-road.w: Look for three deep river gorges running side by side from north to south, between ranges of snowy peaks.
f: Tibetans drank tea churned with butter and salt, so demand was constant.
Old market towns such as Lijiang and Shaxi grew up as caravan stops.
Mule caravans still used parts of the route in the mid-20th century.

q.q: What did Tibet trade for Chinese tea?

tokaido.name: Tōkaidō road
tokaido.t: The old coastal highway from Edo to Kyoto
tokaido.s: In the Edo period the Tōkaidō was Japan's busiest road, running about 500 km along the Pacific coast from Edo, today's Tokyo, to the imperial city of Kyoto. Lords, merchants and pilgrims walked it in about two weeks, stopping at 53 post towns. The artist Hiroshige made it famous in a series of prints. Today the bullet train follows almost the same line, with Mount Fuji watching over it.
tokaido.w: Follow the Pacific coast west from Tokyo; Mount Fuji rises just inland, and the route passes the Hakone hills.
f: Hiroshige's print series 'The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō' appeared in the 1830s.
A barrier at Hakone checked travellers' papers on the road.
Parts of the old stone-paved road still survive near Hakone.

q.q: How many post stations were on the Tōkaidō?

kyoto.name: Kyoto, the old imperial capital
kyoto.t: A thousand years as Japan's capital
kyoto.s: From 794 to 1868 Kyoto was the seat of Japan's emperors. Laid out on a grid modelled on the Chinese capital Chang'an, it became the heart of Japanese court culture: temples, gardens, tea ceremony and the tale of Genji. It still holds well over a thousand Buddhist temples and hundreds of Shinto shrines. From above, look for the city filling a flat basin ringed by wooded mountains, with Lake Biwa to the east.
kyoto.w: Look for a city in a flat basin closed by mountains on three sides, with the large Lake Biwa just to the east.
f: When founded in 794, the city was named Heian-kyō, 'capital of peace'.
UNESCO's listing for ancient Kyoto covers 17 temples, shrines and a castle.
Its streets still follow the grid laid out more than 1,200 years ago.

q.q: What was Kyoto called when it was founded in 794?

nara.name: Nara
nara.t: Japan's first permanent capital and its Great Buddha
nara.s: In 710 Japan's court settled in Nara, its first permanent capital, and for most of the 8th century it was the eastern end of the Silk Road. Buddhism flourished, and Emperor Shōmu cast a giant bronze Buddha and housed it in a vast wooden hall at Tōdai-ji. Tame deer still wander its parks. From above, look for a smaller city in a green basin south of Kyoto.
nara.w: Look for a city in a green basin about 40 km south of Kyoto, backed by wooded hills to the east.
f: The Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji, cast in 752, is about 15 m tall.
Its hall is one of the largest wooden buildings in the world.
Nearby Hōryū-ji contains some of the oldest wooden buildings in the world.

q.q: Which animals roam freely in Nara's parks?

gyeongju.name: Gyeongju
gyeongju.s: For almost a thousand years Gyeongju was the capital of the Korean kingdom of Silla, which united most of the peninsula in the 7th century. Its royal tombs are grassy hills right in the city, and nearby stand the temple of Bulguksa and the stone Buddha of Seokguram. Koreans call it a museum without walls. From above, look for a city in a green basin near the east coast.
gyeongju.w: Look for a city in a green basin among hills near Korea's south-east coast, north of Ulsan.
f: Cheomseongdae, a 7th-century stone tower, is one of the oldest surviving observatories in East Asia.
Gold crowns found in its tombs are among Korea's national treasures.
Bulguksa and Seokguram became UNESCO World Heritage sites in 1995.

q.q: Which kingdom had its capital at Gyeongju?

xian-changan.name: Chang'an and the Terracotta Army
xian-changan.t: The start of the Silk Road and an army of clay
xian-changan.s: Today's Xi'an was Chang'an, capital of the Qin, Han and Tang dynasties and the eastern starting point of the Silk Road. Under the Tang it may have been the largest city in the world. Just east lies the tomb of China's first emperor, guarded by thousands of life-size clay soldiers. From above, look for the city's grid on the Wei river plain, with the Qinling mountains rising to the south.
xian-changan.w: Look for a large grid-planned city on the flat Wei river plain, with the Qinling range rising steeply to the south.
f: The Terracotta Army was found in 1974 by farmers digging a well.
Archaeologists estimate there are around 8,000 figures, their faces individually finished.
Xi'an's Ming city wall, about 14 km around, still stands complete.

q.q: Who found the Terracotta Army in 1974?

forbidden-city.name: Forbidden City, Beijing
forbidden-city.s: At the heart of Beijing lies the Forbidden City, the palace of the Ming and Qing emperors from 1420 to 1912. Walled and moated, it holds some 980 buildings under yellow-tiled roofs, and ordinary people could not enter without permission. It sits exactly on the axis that runs through the old city. In clear air its rectangle can be picked out in the middle of Beijing's grid.
forbidden-city.w: In clear weather, look for a large rectangle at the exact centre of Beijing, with a park and hill on its north side.
f: Twenty-four emperors lived here over almost 500 years.
It is the largest surviving palace complex in the world.
Its yellow roof tiles were a colour reserved for the emperor.

q.q: How many emperors lived in the Forbidden City?

anyang-yinxu.name: Yinxu, the Shang capital
anyang-yinxu.t: Where the oldest Chinese writing was found
anyang-yinxu.s: Near today's Anyang on the North China Plain lay the last capital of the Shang dynasty. Its kings asked questions of their ancestors by cracking bones and turtle shells with heat, then carved the questions and answers on them. These oracle bones are the oldest mature Chinese writing, and many of their characters can still be recognised today. From above, look for the flat, intensely farmed plain north of the Yellow River.
anyang-yinxu.w: Look for the flat, densely farmed North China Plain, with the Taihang mountains rising to the west.
f: Oracle bones were identified in 1899, when a scholar noticed writing on 'dragon bones' sold as medicine.
The intact tomb of Fu Hao, a Shang queen and military leader, was found here in 1976.
Yinxu became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2006.

q.q: On what are the oldest Chinese writings from Yinxu?

dunhuang-mogao.name: Mogao Caves, Dunhuang
dunhuang-mogao.t: A thousand years of Buddhist art in the desert
dunhuang-mogao.s: Where the Silk Road entered China from the western deserts lies the oasis of Dunhuang. In a cliff nearby, monks and patrons carved hundreds of cave shrines over a thousand years and covered them with murals and statues. A sealed library cave, opened in 1900, held tens of thousands of manuscripts. From above, look for the green oasis pressed against enormous golden sand dunes.
dunhuang-mogao.w: Look for a small green oasis pressed against a range of huge golden sand dunes, south of the town of Dunhuang.
f: About 490 caves still hold murals and sculptures.
The library cave held the Diamond Sutra of 868, the oldest dated printed book known.
The Mogao Caves became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1987.

q.q: Which dated printed book was found at Mogao?

qufu.name: Qufu, home of Confucius
qufu.t: The hometown of Confucius and his descendants
qufu.s: In this small city on the Shandong plain, Confucius was born in 551 BC. After his death his house became a temple, and over the centuries emperors enlarged it into one of China's grandest complexes. His descendants lived beside it in a family mansion, and are buried in a vast forest cemetery. From above, look for the flat plain south of Mount Tai, the sacred mountain about 70 km to the north.
qufu.w: Look for the flat Shandong plain, with the sacred Mount Tai rising alone about 70 km to the north.
f: The Kong family tree records more than 80 generations of descendants.
The Confucius family cemetery has been in use for over 2,000 years.
Qufu's temple, mansion and cemetery became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1994.

turpan-jiaohe.name: Turpan oasis: Jiaohe and the karez
turpan-jiaohe.t: An oasis below sea level, watered from underground
turpan-jiaohe.s: The Turpan basin is one of the lowest and hottest places in Asia, yet it is green with vineyards. The secret is the karez: tunnels dug to carry snowmelt from the Tian Shan underground, safe from evaporation. On a narrow island between two rivers stand the ruins of Jiaohe, a Silk Road city carved down into the earth. From above, look for the red Flaming Mountains and the oasis beside them.
turpan-jiaohe.w: Look for a deep desert basin with a long red ridge, the Flaming Mountains, and green oasis fields along it.
f: The lowest point of the basin lies about 150 m below sea level.
Turpan's karez tunnels together run for thousands of kilometres.
Much of Jiaohe was built by digging rooms out of the ground rather than building upward.

loulan.name: Loulan
loulan.t: A lost oasis kingdom at the edge of Lop Nur
loulan.s: On the shores of Lop Nur, once a lake at the eastern end of the Tarim basin, stood Loulan, a small kingdom on the Silk Road. When the rivers shifted and the lake shrank, the city was left to the desert, and sand buried its houses and records. From above, look for the vast dry bed of Lop Nur, whose pale concentric rings look like a giant ear.
loulan.w: Look for a huge pale lakebed with concentric rings like an ear, in the desert east of the Taklamakan.
f: The Swedish explorer Sven Hedin found Loulan's ruins in 1900.
Documents found there are written on wood and paper in several languages.
The 'Ear of Lop Nur' rings are shorelines left as the lake dried.

karakorum.name: Karakorum
karakorum.t: Capital of the Mongol Empire on the open steppe
karakorum.s: In the green Orkhon valley of central Mongolia stood Karakorum, capital of the Mongol Empire in the mid-13th century. Envoys, merchants and craftsmen came from Europe, Persia and China. A European friar who visited in 1254 described a silver tree in the khan's palace that poured out drinks. Little is left today, but the wide Orkhon valley and its rolling steppe are easy to see.
karakorum.w: Look for the broad green Orkhon river valley on open steppe, with forested Khangai mountains to the west.
f: The silver drinking fountain was made by a goldsmith from Paris, Guillaume Boucher.
The Erdene Zuu monastery was built in 1585, partly from the city's ruins.
The Orkhon valley became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2004.
